verified.title: Printable-ASCII ground-run scan (the parser's only remaining per-byte loop on ASCII text)
verified.simd_shape: Range test folds to one unsigned compare: `(byte &- 0x20) < 0x5F`. Vector form: while `index + 16 <= bytes.count`, load `SIMD16<UInt8>` from `bytes.baseAddress! + index` (via `UnsafeRawPointer(...).loadUnaligned(as: SIMD16<UInt8>.self)`), compute `let bad = (v &- 0x20) .>= 0x5F`; if `!any(bad)` advance 16 and continue, else fall into the existing scalar loop for that final block. Tail (<16 bytes) stays scalar. No movemask/first-set-lane primitive is needed, which matters because Swift's SIMDMask has no portable bit-extract.
verified.hot_path_evidence: `research/10/F6` puts `TerminalInputStream.feed` at 8.7-9.0% (styled-screen-redraw) and 11.8% (incremental-screen-updates) inclusive of the harness root, `EscapeAbsorber.consume` at 3.4-6.0%; `research/10/F1` states outright that "parsing is not the bottleneck". Both profiles predate `T8`, when every byte still went through the UTF-8 DFA -- today ASCII bytes bypass the decoder entirely and this scan is the only per-byte parser work they pay, so the residual is a fraction of that 9-12%. `research/33/F10` sizes the loop's trip count directly: mean ASCII run 44.8 (scrollback-stream), 32.2 (styled-screen-redraw), 23.8 (unicode-wrapping), 12.2 (synchronized-frames), 8.3 (incremental-screen-updates); longest run 25-177.
verified.risks: Arithmetic caps the win. The loop visits each printable byte once with a load + two compares + increment (~1-1.5 cycles/byte with good ILP); scrollback-stream's 1.5M printed characters is therefore ~2M cycles, ~0.6 ms, against a drain `research/33/F16` measured at 70.5 ms -- roughly 1%. Even a generous reading of `research/10/F6`'s 9-12% parser share puts the ceiling at 2-4% on `terminal-feed`, straddling the 2.5% `quick` / 1.85% `confirm` thresholds, so a paired A/B may well read `inconclusive`. Two of the five corpora have mean runs of 8.3 and 12.2 bytes, where a 16-lane block never completes and the change is pure overhead -- so the vector path must be gated on remaining length, not entered blind. Correctness risks are small but real: no overread past `bytes.count` is permitted (the buffer is `base + filled` inside the host's turn storage and may abut its end), and the run boundary is observable -- `TerminalStreamAction.printASCIIRun` is documented as "one GL print per byte", and `TerminalASCIIRunTests` plus the 67-fixture chunk-boundary replay pin that a run cut anywhere still produces the identical token stream, so an off-by-one is caught but must be tested at every offset mod 16.

impact_review.verdict: On the hot path but arithmetically tiny. Every printable ASCII byte in every workload passes through this loop, so it is not off the profile — but post-T8/T7 it is two compares and an increment per byte, and the same byte is then touched at least twice more by much heavier downstream loops. A perfect SIMD scan plausibly buys ~0.3-0.8% on the best-case headline workload (scrollback-stream), below both the 2.5% `quick` and 1.85% `confirm` directional thresholds. Not worth scheduling on impact grounds; a paired A/B would most likely read `inconclusive` or `equivalent`.
impact_review.evidence:
CODE (verified, /Users/dan/Code/danterm/lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalInputStream.swift:86-89 and :50-52): the cited loop exists exactly as quoted. `bytes` is an `UnsafeBufferPointer<UInt8>`, so in `-O` the subscript carries no bounds check and the loop is load + `>=`/`<=` + increment + a well-predicted branch, ~1-1.5 cycles/byte. It is a search loop with a data-dependent exit, which LLVM does not auto-vectorize, so the scalar form is what runs today.

WHAT ELSE TOUCHES THE SAME BYTE (Terminal.swift:7639-7662, 7755-7820, 7835+): per run the engine does (a) this parser scan, (b) `printASCIIRun`'s outer loop, (c) `printBulkNarrow`'s per-cell `cells[column+count].kind` scan over the destination row, (d) `writeNarrowCells` stamping a CellWord per cell, plus one `invalidateInspection`, one content-identity allocation, one `rememberOpenCluster`, one damage snapshot diff per run. The parser scan is the cheapest of the three per-element loops on the ASCII path. Vectorizing it alone caps the win at its own share.

PROFILE SIZING. `33/F16` gives the only post-T8 wall-clock anchor: scrollback-stream drain 70.5 ms for 1,525,000 corpus bytes / 1,500,000 printed cells (21.6 MB/s). At ~4 GHz that is ~280M cycles, ~185 cycles per printed cell. `33/F16`'s own run table puts 1,491,667 of those bytes inside runs. At 1.5 cycles/byte the scan is ~2.2M cycles = **~0.8% of the drain**; a 16-lane version at ~0.2 cycles/byte recovers ~1.7M cycles = **~0.6% end-to-end**, on the corpus with the longest runs (mean 44.8). That is the ceiling, not the expectation.

RUN-LENGTH GATING (`33/F10`, `33/F16` agree to the unit): mean run 44.8 / 32.2 / 23.8 / 12.2 / 8.3 across the five corpora; longest 25 on incremental-screen-updates. Two of five corpora never complete a 16-lane block on the mean, and `incremental-screen-updates` — where `TerminalInputStream.feed` scored highest in the old profiles — has the *shortest* runs, so it is the worst case for the vector path, not the best.

WHY THE OLD 9-12% NUMBER DOES NOT TRANSFER: `10/F6`'s 8.7-9.0% / 11.8% and `10/F1`'s 7.1/6.8/11.1% for `TerminalInputStream.feed` are inclusive figures from a build where every byte went through the UTF-8 DFA, the absorber was consulted per byte, and each token was materialized into an eager array (`33/F9`, `33/F15`). `33/F16` and `33/F17` deleted all three for ASCII. `10/F1`'s own inference is "parsing is not the bottleneck" even at that share; today's ASCII residual is a small fraction of it.

NO CONTRARY EVIDENCE: `17` (CPU sweep) never names `TerminalInputStream` or `isPrintableASCII`; the only parser mention is `17/F14`'s note that "the per-byte array frames under [applyOutput] are the parser loop", in a finding whose headline result is that frame-subtraction sizing of that region is unsound under partial inlining. Nothing in `19`, `20`, `28`, or `31` attributes measurable time to this scan.
impact_review.corrections:
1. Citation drift on the profile share: the finder attributes "parsing is not the bottleneck" to `10/F1` (correct) and the 8.7-11.8% to `10/F6` (also correct) — but it then treats that inclusive, pre-T7/T8 figure as a live ceiling and derives "2-4% on terminal-feed". That ceiling is stale by roughly an order of magnitude: the DFA, per-byte absorber consultation, and the eager action array that made up most of that node are gone from the ASCII path. The honest ceiling from the only post-T8 measurement (`33/F16`, 70.5 ms drain) is under 1%.

2. `estimated_impact: "low"` is right, but `confidence: "medium"` is understated in the pessimistic direction — the arithmetic is not uncertain. The drain figure, the byte counts, and the run structure are all exact and independently cross-checked (`33/F10` and `33/F16` agree to the unit on five corpora). This is a confident "too small", not an uncertain "maybe small".

3. "The parser's only remaining per-byte loop on ASCII text" is true of the parser, but the framing invites over-reading. `printScalarRun` (Terminal.swift:7666) has its own per-byte continuation-count loop for non-ASCII, and `printBulkNarrow`'s destination `kind` scan (Terminal.swift:7777-7785) is a per-cell loop over the same span that is a strictly better SIMD target — it reads packed cell words and is on the same run. If any SIMD work is scheduled on this path, that loop and the cell-write loop dominate the scan.

4. The risks section says a 16-lane block "never completes" at mean 8.3-12.2 and so the vector path must be length-gated. Correct, but it understates the consequence: with a `index + 16 <= count` gate the vector path is simply never entered on `incremental-screen-updates` (longest run 25, mean 8.3) beyond at most one block, so the two workloads where `10/F6` measured the parser highest are the two where this change does nothing.

5. Minor: `data_layout_ready: true` is accurate — `bytes` is already an `UnsafeBufferPointer`, no CoW or Array bounds-check obstacle exists at this site. That is the one part of the candidate that needs no qualification, and it is also why the scalar loop is already near-optimal.

confidence_review.verdict: FEASIBILITY CONFIRMED, VALUE REFUTED. I could not refute the vectorizability: this is the cleanest SIMD target in the tree that I checked. The data is contiguous `UnsafeBufferPointer<UInt8>` end to end, there is no Array indexing, no CoW, no bounds check in -O, and the predicate is stateless per byte, so block-wise processing has zero semantic interaction with the things the lens asks about (UTF-8 resumption, chunk boundaries, replacement, wide cells, clusters all live outside the loop). The proposed shape is correct as written and can be made slightly better than proposed. What does not survive scrutiny is the payoff: the finder sized the scan against the whole drain but never against the per-byte work in the consumer of the same run, and once you do that the ceiling drops below its own 1% estimate. It is a ~1-cycle-per-byte loop feeding a path that spends 10-20 cycles per byte immediately afterwards on the same bytes. Feasible and almost certainly unmeasurable.
confidence_review.evidence:
DATA LAYOUT -- confirmed clean, no blockers.
- /Users/dan/Code/danterm/lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalInputStream.swift:74-88. `nextAction(in bytes: UnsafeBufferPointer<UInt8>, from index: inout Int)`. `bytes[index]` on `UnsafeBufferPointer` is `_debugPrecondition`-guarded only, so there is no bounds check in a release build and no CoW check anywhere. `bytes.baseAddress` is directly available.
- Both producers are already contiguous: /Users/dan/Code/danterm/lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift:1833-1848 (`feed([UInt8])` -> `withUnsafeBufferPointer`, plus a public `feed(UnsafeBufferPointer<UInt8>)`), and /Users/dan/Code/danterm/lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift:2149-2158 (`turnStorage.withUnsafeMutableBufferPointer`). Nothing to restructure before vectorizing.

SEMANTICS -- no block-wise hazard.
- The scan runs only under `absorber.isGround, decoder.isIdle` (line 85), and the comment at 80-84 states the invariant holds for the whole run because neither absorber nor decoder is consulted inside it. So there is no carried state a 16-byte block could desynchronize.
- Chunk boundaries are already a non-issue by contract: the run stops at `bytes.count` and `.printASCIIRun` is documented (TerminalInputStream.swift:13-17) as "one GL print per byte", so a run cut anywhere is behaviorally identical. The vector rewrite does not change where runs are cut at all -- it computes the same maximal-run predicate.
- Everything the lens worries about (wide cells, clusters, insert mode, pending wrap, identity-wrap straddle) is enforced downstream in `printBulkNarrow` (Terminal.swift:7755-7797), not in the scan. The parser cannot get those wrong.

OVERREAD -- the constraint is real, and the proposed gate handles it.
- TerminalPTYHost.swift:2158 feeds `UnsafeBufferPointer(start: base + filled, count: result)` out of a 16 KB `turnStorage` (line 388, 456). When `filled + result == cap == storage.count` the fed slice ends exactly at the Array's last byte, so a blind 16-byte load past `count` is genuinely out of bounds. Gating on `index + 16 <= bytes.count` is mandatory, not defensive.

WHY THE WIN IS SMALLER THAN CLAIMED.
- The same bytes are walked at least twice more after the scan. `printASCIIRun` (Terminal.swift:7639-7663) re-reads each byte through the `printBulkNarrow` supplier closure; `printBulkNarrow` (7777-7785) runs a second per-byte loop reading `cells[column + count].kind` over 16-byte `GridCell` elements; `writeNarrowCells` (7848-7860) constructs a `GridCell` per byte (two live `precondition`s survive -O, see Terminal.swift:221-227) and stores 16 bytes. `GridCell` is `CellWord` (UInt64) + `ContentIdentity` (UInt32, Terminal.swift:193) + `HyperlinkId` (UInt16, line 183) = 16-byte stride. That is roughly 10-20 cycles per byte against the scan's ~1.
- So the honest ceiling is a few percent of the ASCII print path, not a few percent of `research/10/F6`'s 7-12% parser share -- and those percentages are for the pre-`T7`/`T8` `TerminalInputStream.feed`, which also built the 32-byte-per-token action array that `F9`/`F15` sized at 60-80x the corpus byte count. `F16` (drain 153.2 ms -> 70.5 ms on scrollback-stream) deleted most of what those samples were measuring.
- Run lengths bound it further: `33/F10` and `F16` both give mean 44.8 / longest 60 (scrollback-stream), and mean 8.3 / longest 25 (incremental-screen-updates), mean 12.2 (synchronized-frames). At mean 44.8 a 16-lane block saves ~30 scalar iterations out of a run that costs ~450+ cycles downstream.

CODEGEN SENSITIVITY -- a real risk the finder does not mention.
- Terminal.swift:1870-1872 carries `@inline(never)` on `apply` with the note "from measurement, not taste: letting the optimizer inline this dispatch into the pull loop cost a further 1.5 points on the drain (`research/33/F15`)". A vector prologue at the top of `nextAction` is exactly the kind of code-size change that has already been shown to move this loop by more than the arithmetic predicts -- in either direction.
confidence_review.corrections:
1. "No movemask/first-set-lane primitive is needed, which matters because Swift's SIMDMask has no portable bit-extract" -- the premise is wrong, and the workaround it forces is unnecessary. A portable first-bad-lane exists in the stdlib: build `SIMD16<UInt8>(0,1,...,15)`, `.replacing(with: SIMD16(repeating: 255), where: bad)`, then the `.min()` reduction. Three vector ops, no scalar re-scan of the failing block. The finder's "fall into the existing scalar loop for that final block" costs up to 15 redundant scalar iterations on *every* run end, which is precisely the corpora (mean run 8.3 and 12.2) where it claims the change is already pure overhead.

2. The test-coverage claim is wrong in both directions. `TerminalFixtureTests.splitStrategies` (/Users/dan/Code/danterm/lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalFixtureTests.swift:447-460) does not split feeds "at 7 bytes" -- it splits each feed event at a *single* offset, exhaustively at `0...bytes.count` for every event <= 64 bytes and for every windows-terminal fixture. That is far better mod-16 alignment coverage than the finder credits. Conversely the suite the finder names as the guard, `TerminalASCIIRunTests`, uses `chunkSizes = [1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 64]` (line 23), so six of its seven chunkings can never enter a 16-lane block at all -- only 64 can. A vector path would land essentially untested by the suite written for this feature unless new chunk sizes (16, 17, 31) are added.

3. "Bounds checks and Array CoW block auto-vectorization" is not what blocks it here -- there are neither. What blocks LLVM is the data-dependent early exit: this is an uncounted search loop, and LLVM's loop vectorizer does not vectorize early-exit loops. That is worth stating positively, because it removes the lens's "would an auto-vectorizable rewrite already capture the win" escape hatch -- it would not, and there is no memset/memcpy/`initialize(repeating:)` analogue for a search. Explicit SIMD (or SWAR over UInt64, which is messier here because the [0x20,0x7E] range test needs the masked no-borrow form) is the only route.

4. `estimated_impact: "low"` is still generous. The finder's own ~0.85% figure for scrollback-stream should be read as an upper bound, not a midpoint, because it charges the scan nothing for the fact that the consumer immediately re-walks the same bytes at ~10-20x the cost. On `incremental-screen-updates` and `synchronized-frames` the expected sign is negative before the first-lane fix in correction 1.

5. Minor: `research/10`'s findings are in a flat file, /Users/dan/Code/danterm/docs/research/10-terminal-feed-hotspots.md, not a directory -- the "F6" citation lands on the tables at lines 533, 1000 and 1175, which read 7.1-11.8% for `TerminalInputStream.feed(_:)`. Those are pre-`T7`/`T8` and include the deleted action array; citing them as today's parser share overstates the residual by a large factor.

verified.title: Continuation-byte counting scan in printScalarRun -- a third pass over bytes already decoded twice
verified.simd_shape: Counting scalar starts is `popcount((b & 0xC0) != 0x80)` over the block. Vector form: load `SIMD16<UInt8>`, `let starts = (v & 0xC0) .!= 0x80`, add `SIMD16<UInt8>(repeating: 0).replacing(with: 1, where: starts)` into a running `SIMD16<UInt8>` accumulator (flush to a wider accumulator every 255 blocks) and take `.wrappedSum()`; only when the running total could cross `columnCount` do you drop into the scalar loop to find the exact cut. Both scan bounds are loop-invariant, so a whole 16-byte block is either entirely below the cap or is the block that straddles it.
verified.hot_path_evidence: Reached only from `.printScalarRun`, i.e. non-ASCII text. `research/33/F10` shows `unicode-wrapping` carries 1,208,250 of 1,305,000 prints inside runs at mean 23.8; no profile in docs/research attributes time to this specific loop (it postdates doc 10's captures and no post-`T8` feed profile exists). So: plausibly warm on `unicode-wrapping`, no direct profile evidence.
verified.risks: The ideal fix deletes this loop rather than vectorizing it, and per the design bar that option should stay on the table. `TerminalInputStream.nextAction` (TerminalInputStream.swift:98-124) already walks the run scalar by scalar to decide its extent, so it knows the scalar count for free; `printScalarRun` then rescans to count and decodes a *third* time through a fresh `UTF8Decoder` inside `printBulkNarrow`'s supplier. Widening the action to `.printScalarRun(range:scalarCount:)` removes pass 2 entirely at zero runtime cost and keeps the action POD. SIMD here would be optimizing a pass that should not exist. If the loop survives for another reason, the `scalarCount < columnCount` cap is a genuine data-dependent exit, so LLVM will not auto-vectorize it and the work must be hand-written.

impact_review.verdict: Essentially off the profile. The loop is real and correctly cited, but it is reached by only ~2.6% of `terminal-feed`'s bytes and by zero bytes of every other calibrated workload. A SIMD rewrite is worth low single-digit *microseconds* on a ~17 MB feed -- far under measurement noise, and strictly dominated by the "delete the loop" fix the candidate itself names.

The `hot_path_evidence` is misattributed. `research/33/F10`'s "unicode-wrapping carries 1,208,250 of 1,305,000 prints inside runs at mean 23.8" is the **ASCII-run** table (docs/research/33-by-construction-perf-survey/findings.md:390-396) -- those runs feed `printASCIIRun`, which has no counting loop. confidence_review.verdict: Feasible but not worth doing. On pure vectorizability this loop is near-ideal: it reads a contiguous `UnsafeBufferPointer<UInt8>` (no Array, no CoW, no release-mode bounds checks), and every semantic hazard the lens asks about is already excluded upstream. But the candidate's own risk section is the right answer: `scan`'s final value is dead, so the loop's only product is a capped count that `TerminalInputStream.nextAction` already knows for free, and `printBulkNarrow` already clamps to the row. Delete the pass, don't vectorize it. Even if it survived, a single-exit rewrite auto-vectorizes without hand SIMD, and the payoff is bounded by <= ~3% of prints on the most Unicode-heavy corpus in the tree. confidence_review.evidence:
CODE (verified, Terminal.swift:7666-7695): the counting loop is at 7672-7677, exactly as quoted.

Feasibility, in favor:
- Data is `UnsafeBufferPointer<UInt8>` handed down from `Terminal.feed` (Terminal.swift:1883-1884) into `printScalarRun(bytes, range)`. Contiguous, borrowed, no Array indexing, no CoW check, `UnsafeBufferPointer.subscript` is `_debugPrecondition`-only so release has no bounds check. A 16-byte `loadUnaligned(fromByteOffset:as: SIMD16<UInt8>.self)` is legal and cheap here.
- Every semantic hazard is excluded *before* the range is formed. `TerminalInputStream.nextAction` (TerminalInputStream.swift:88-131) only extends `runEnd` past a scalar that (a) started at `bytes[probeIndex] >= 0x80`, so the range contains zero ASCII bytes; (b) decoded completely with `consumedEveryByte` and `probeIndex - scalarStart == encodedByteCount`, so the range holds only well-formed UTF-8 and can never contain a replacement/maximal-subpart case; (c) is `isBulkPrintable`, so no wide cells, no emoji, grapheme class `.other` only, so no cluster joining inside the run. `runEnd` is always a scalar boundary, so no chunk-boundary or resumability concern: the decoder state that crosses feeds lives in `TerminalInputStream.decoder`, never inside the range. Counting `(b & 0xC0) != 0x80` over the block is therefore exact, block-wise, and order-free.
- The two bounds are loop-invariant; the only tail work is <16 bytes plus the block that straddles the cap.

Feasibility, against:
- The `scalarCount < columnCount` cap is a reduction-dependent second exit, so LLVM will not auto-vectorize the loop as written (candidate is correct on this).
- Typical trip count is small. Runs here are narrow non-ASCII only, i.e. the gaps between ASCII runs; at 2-3 bytes/scalar a whole run is often under one 16-byte block, so accumulator setup + `wrappedSum` + tail can cost more than the scalar loop it replaces.

Value (this is what sinks it):
- No profile in docs/research attributes any time to this loop; the candidate concedes this.
- Bounding its share from research/33 F10 (findings.md:384-413): on `unicode-wrapping`, prints = 1,305,000, prints inside ASCII runs = 1,208,250, wide prints = 54,000. So prints reaching `printScalarRun` are at most ~42,750, about 3% of prints, on the corpus purpose-built to be Unicode-heavy. The loop touches roughly those scalars' bytes, once, at ~1 op/byte.
- Of the three passes over these bytes (nextAction's decode, this count, printBulkNarrow's supplier decode via a fresh `UTF8Decoder`), this is the cheapest. Vectorizing it leaves both DFA passes untouched.

Ideal fix confirmed against the code: `printBulkNarrow` computes `let available = min(runCount, columnCount - column)` (Terminal.swift:7776) and then further trims to the first non-`.narrow`/`.padding` cell, so an oversized `runCount` is already clamped -- the cap in the counting loop exists only so the count never overstates the scalars actually present in the range. Widening the action to `.printScalarRun(range:scalarCount:)` and tracking `remaining -= taken` (and `-= 1` on the decline branch) is exactly correct, keeps the action POD, and deletes pass 2 outright.
confidence_review.corrections:
1. Misattributed hot-path evidence. `research/33/F10`'s "1,208,250 of 1,305,000 prints inside runs at mean 23.8" is the **ASCII-run** table (findings.md:396), explicitly "cut ... at a non-ASCII scalar" -- it describes `printASCIIRun`, not `printScalarRun`. Read correctly it bounds this loop's reach *downward*: at most ~42,750 prints (1,305,000 - 1,208,250 - 54,000 wide) can reach `printScalarRun` on `unicode-wrapping`, ~3% of prints. The candidate cites it as evidence the loop is "plausibly warm"; it is evidence the loop is cold even on the Unicode corpus.

2. The candidate calls this "a third pass over bytes already decoded twice" but does not note that `scan`'s final value is never read -- only `scalarCount` escapes the loop. That matters twice over: it is why the fix is a plain count carried forward (no cut position to reconstruct), and it is why the "find the exact cut" scalar fallback in the proposed SIMD shape is unnecessary work.

3. "LLVM will not auto-vectorize it and the work must be hand-written" is half right. The cap does block it as written, but the loop does not need the cap to be exact: scanning a fixed byte window (`min(range.upperBound, index + 2 * columnCount)` -- every scalar here is >= 2 bytes) and then `min(count, columnCount)` is a single-exit reduction that arm64 LLVM vectorizes on its own, and truncating the window mid-scalar can only under-count, never over-count, so it stays safe for `printBulkNarrow`. So even in the world where the loop survives, hand-written SIMD is not the required tool.

4. `data_layout_ready: true` is right, but the reason is upstream, not local: the guarantees come from `nextAction`'s probe loop, not from anything visible at Terminal.swift:7672. Anyone acting on this must keep those three guards (>= 0x80, `consumedEveryByte` + byte-count match, `isBulkPrintable`) in view, since a future relaxation of `isBulkPrintable` to admit wide scalars would not break the count but would break the "one scalar, one narrow cell" assumption the count feeds.

verified.simd_shape: The only vectorizable half is find-and-validate: a SIMD16 scan for the first byte < 0x80 bounds the run in one pass, and a simdutf/lemire-style block validator (three shifted lookups over leading/continuation nibbles) can confirm a 16-byte block is well-formed UTF-8 and count its scalar starts without stepping the DFA. STRUCTURAL FEASIBILITY -- confirmed, no blockers.

Source is already contiguous and unsafe. `TerminalInputStream.nextAction(in bytes: UnsafeBufferPointer<UInt8>, from index: inout Int)` (/Users/dan/Code/danterm/lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalInputStream.swift:74-77) hands the absorber a raw buffer; `UnsafeBufferPointer.subscript` is `_debugPrecondition`-guarded, so release builds have no bounds check. The neighbouring ASCII-run and scalar-run loops (lines 87, 98) already scan this same buffer, so the bulk-run shape is precedent, not a new idea.

No CoW hazard on the destination. `Terminal.swift:948` holds `private var inputStream = TerminalInputStream()` and `Terminal.swift:1858/1867` mutate it in place; nothing copies the absorber mid-feed. So `controlStringPayload` is uniquely referenced while collecting, and the per-byte `Array.append` pays a uniqueness check + capacity check + count store per byte, not a buffer copy per byte. A bulk `append(contentsOf: UnsafeBufferPointer(rebasing:))` collapses that to one check plus a memcpy -- correct and easy.

Semantics are the friendliest in the whole candidate set. Control strings bypass the UTF-8 decoder entirely (`nextAction` line 137: `guard absorber.isGround else { ... absorber.consume(byte) }` -- the decoder is never consulted), so there is no resumability, no maximal-subpart replacement, no grapheme or wide-cell question. The payload is opaque bytes. That removes every semantic blocker that sinks candidates 1 and 4.

Chunk invariance is provable rather than risky. A run is by definition N iterations that all take the same branch, and no state other than the payload changes inside it, so any split reproduces byte-identical state. The one place to get it wrong is the capacity latch at EscapeAbsorber.swift:703-710: per byte, the byte arriving at `count == capacity` sets `controlStringPayloadOverflowed = true` and is not appended. Bulk equivalent is `let room = capacity - count; append(prefix(room)); if run.count > room { overflowed = true }` -- exact, but it must be written that way.

STOP SETS -- the candidate got one of them wrong.

`.oscString` (EscapeAbsorber.swift:357-372): 0x07/0x18/0x1A/0x1B stop; 0x00-0x06, 0x08-0x17, 0x19, 0x1C-0x1F, 0x7F are silently dropped without leaving the state; **0x20-0x7E and 0x80-0xFF are payload**. The code says so itself at lines 412-414: "0x9C inside an OSC payload is UTF-8 continuation data (U+201C is E2 80 9C), not a terminator". The correct mask is `(b .< 0x20) | (b .== 0x7F)`.

`.dcsPassthrough` with a route (lines 381-393): stop set is exactly {0x18, 0x1A, 0x1B}; everything else including C0 and high bytes is collected verbatim (DCSSequence doc comment, lines 43-45).

`.sosPmApcString` and unrouted `.dcsPassthrough`/`.dcsIgnore`: line 400 `if isNonOSCControlString, byte >= 0x80 { return nil }` filters every high byte before the switch, so the stop set is again just {0x18, 0x1A, 0x1B}. Three equality compares -- trivially vectorizable, and no append at all.

The discard sub-case is bigger than the candidate says. `DCSRoute.init?` (lines 23-30) routes only `$q` (DECRQSS) and `+q` (XTGETTCAP) -- both replies of tens of bytes. docs/terminal-capabilities.md:245 confirms "tmux control mode, sixel, DECDLD soft fonts, DECRQUPSS, and DECDMAC" are all unrouted. Their bodies therefore do not take the short routed early-return at line 381 (it requires `dcsRoute != nil`); they fall through the >=0x80 guard, the full nine-case `switch byte`, and then the `switch state` to `case .dcsPassthrough: return nil` at line 609 -- the longest per-byte chain in the file, run once per body byte, to produce nothing. That is the sub-case with a 3-byte stop set, zero appends, no overflow latch, and no interface risk.

WHY IT IS NOT A 9 OR 10.

Most of the win needs no SIMD. On the collect path the per-byte costs are the `consume` call, the two guards, and `Array.append`; a scalar `while` that finds the stop byte and does one `append(contentsOf:)` removes all of them. The remaining memcpy runs at 16-32 B/cycle already. Explicit SIMD only speeds the scan pass, and on the collect path the scan is the cheaper of the two passes. The honest framing is "bulk entry point", with SIMD as an optional inner detail -- and the candidate's own "cheaper first step" note half-recognises this, though it names the wrong cheaper step (hoisting the guards leaves the per-byte `append` and the per-byte call in place; bulk-appending the run is what actually pays).

Where SIMD does earn its place: LLVM's loop vectorizer will not vectorize a search loop with a data-dependent exit, so the scalar scan stays ~1-2 B/cycle. On the pure-discard path, where the scan is the entire cost, explicit SIMD16 is the only way to get 8-16x -- there is no memcpy to hide behind.

HOT PATH -- the candidate's self-assessment is accurate, and I confirm it. docs/research/10-terminal-feed-hotspots.md attributes almost all of `EscapeAbsorber.consume` to CSI dispatch: 538/621, 232/286, and 222/256 samples land under `dispatchCSI` (lines 1045-1046, 888-889, 575-576). Control-string collection is invisible. The benchmark producer rides its sequence number on an OSC title (scripts/terminal-benchmark-producer.py:106) and the corpus carries OSC 7 / OSC 133 prompts -- all sub-200-byte payloads. No workload feeds a large control string.

The candidate's stated justification -- "since high bytes are payload" -- is exactly backwards: because they are payload they must NOT match. The code's own comment at EscapeAbsorber.swift:412-414 spells this out for 0x9C. Best case the run ends at the first UTF-8 lead byte and every non-ASCII title degrades to per-byte (no speedup); worst case an implementer treats the matched high byte as a terminator and truncates the title. Correct mask: `(b .< 0x20) | (b .== 0x7F)`.

2. "`.sosPmApcString` is the same scan" understates the discard case. APC is only one of the discard states, and not the interesting one. The volume case is an *unrouted DCS* body -- sixel, tmux control mode, DECDLD -- which does not take the routed early-return at line 381 and instead walks the >=0x80 guard plus both switches per byte before returning nil at line 609. Same 3-byte stop set, longer per-byte chain, more plausible byte volume.

3. The stop set for a routed DCS is not the same as for OSC. A routed DCS collects C0 and DEL verbatim (line 391, unconditional `collectControlString`), so a shared "control-string scan" would corrupt DECRQSS/XTGETTCAP bodies by dropping bytes the DCSSequence doc comment (lines 43-45) requires be preserved. Hoisting the two guards out of `collectControlString` leaves the per-byte `consume` call and, more importantly, the per-byte `Array.append` -- and the append is the expensive half. The actual cheap step with most of the win is the scalar bulk run plus one `append(contentsOf:)`; SIMD is then an inner optimization of the scan.

At that moment the buffer has two references (the array and the enum payload), so `removeAll(keepingCapacity:)` goes through `_makeUniqueAndReserveCapacityIfNotUnique` and copies the entire payload into a fresh buffer before setting count to 0 -- an O(payload) copy whose result is immediately discarded, on every OSC dispatch. `dispatchDCS` (725-737) has the same shape. There is no workload today, and adding a bulk entry point widens the interface of the one component whose chunk-invariance the 67-fixture replay and `TerminalInputStreamTests` exist to protect. If any of this is done, the ordering that respects the evidence is: (5) first, since it is free; then the scalar bulk run for the unrouted-DCS/APC discard, which needs no append, no latch, and no OSC mask; and only then SIMD, and only behind a workload that actually feeds one.

verified.title: Byte-at-a-time UTF-8 DFA in the non-ASCII scalar-run probe (nextAction)
verified.simd_shape: Replace the per-byte DFA with a block classifier over the non-ASCII byte range, using stdlib SIMD16<UInt8>. Per 16-byte block: (1) lead/continuation mask via (v & 0xC0) .== 0x80, whose complement popcount is the scalar count and whose bit positions are the scalar boundaries; (2) an expected-length vector from the lead bytes (1/2/3/4 from the top nibble) compared against the observed gaps to validate the block in ~6 lane ops instead of ~16 dependent table-indexed state transitions; (3) reconstruct scalar values for the (dominant) uniform-length case with shifts and ORs rather than the accumulator recurrence. Fall back to the existing scalar DFA for any block the validator rejects and for the <=3-byte tail. Independently and as a prerequisite: move UTF8Decoder.characterClasses/transitions out of `static let [UInt8]` (each subscript is a swift_once-guarded global access plus a release-mode Array bounds check) into an InlineArray or a pointer to a static blob, so the residual scalar path is branchless.
verified.hot_path_evidence: Real but narrow, and only one committed workload has it. I decoded benchmarks/fixtures/recordings/synchronized-frames-v1-btop-95-frames.json.gz (the btop capture) and evaluated the committed two-stage table against every scalar in it: 441,483 of 3,020,580 bytes (14.6%) are non-ASCII, forming 147,463 scalars, and ALL 147,463 are bulk-printable (braille U+28xx 57,428 + 13,091 + ..., box-drawing U+2500 40,541, U+25A0 14,261, U+00B0 900 -- every one narrow/.other/no emoji flags). That count matches research/33/F16's post-T8 `terminalUnicodeClassification` count for synchronized-frames to the unit (147,463), which independently confirms the composition. 85% of those scalars sit in runs of >=2 and 57% in runs of >=16 scalars (48+ bytes), longest run 178 scalars / 534 bytes -- a full 179-column row of braille. So this loop walks ~441K bytes per replay on this corpus. No published profile covers it: doc 17's sweep (2026-07-29) and doc 10 (2026-07-28) both predate the ASCII-run change (research/33/F16, 2026-08-07) and the scalar-run change (plans/impl/2026-08-20-0011-scalar-bulk-print-runs.md), and neither sweep includes synchronized-frames or unicode-wrapping as a traced workload. Counter-evidence for the other four corpora: scrollback-stream, styled-screen-redraw and incremental-screen-updates are 0.00% non-ASCII, so this loop never runs on them at all; unicode-wrapping is 19.5% non-ASCII but every one of its non-ASCII scalars (CJK wide, U+0301 zero-width, the ZWJ emoji sequence, U+1F680) fails `isBulkPrintable`, so its non-ASCII runs are 2-15 bytes and the probe decodes one scalar and bails.
verified.risks: The run boundary is not 'valid UTF-8', it is 'valid UTF-8 AND bulk-printable AND not a C1 control', and bulk-printability is a two-stage table gather that no ARM SIMD instruction helps with -- so the vector work removes only the DFA half and ~3 dependent loads per scalar survive. On btop content the runs are homogeneous 3-byte sequences inside one 128-scalar stage-one block, which means the cheaper non-SIMD win (hoist the stage-one block index across the run, cache the last classification) may capture most of the same time with a fraction of the code. Correctness risk is the maximal-subpart contract: any block the vector validator does not accept in full must re-run the scalar DFA from the block start so error positions and replacement counts are bit-identical, and the block must never claim a trailing partial sequence -- back off to the last complete scalar boundary (at most 3 bytes) and let the resumable decoder own the tail. Both are satisfiable, but the 67-fixture replay that splits feeds at 7 bytes is the gate. Also: this path is <3 weeks old and unprofiled; measure `just benchmark-quick baseline=HEAD workload=synchronized-frames` before writing any of it.

The finder's proposed structural check ((v & 0xC0) .== 0x80 plus expected-length-from-top-nibble) accepts overlongs (E0 80 80), surrogates (ED A0 80), and F5..FF, i.e. it is not a validator. Correct range checks by compare-mask, plus per-block scalar-phase carry, is realistically 20-40 ops/16B, not ~6.
2. Predicate is semantic, not structural, and has THREE parts, not one. Besides isBulkPrintable the loop honors isIgnoredDecodedScalar (U+0080-U+009F), which does `continue input` and commits `decoder = probe` -- so a structurally valid block can still need a mid-block break on a decoded value. isBulkPrintable is 3 dependent Array loads: UnicodeProperties.generated.swift:3038 `stageOne[Int(value >> 7)]` then `stageTwo[(block << 7) | Int(value & 0x7F)]` then `palette[...]`, followed by 5 field comparisons on a multi-field struct (UnicodeBulkPrinting.swift). At 3-byte btop scalars that is ~5.3 serial gathers per 16-byte block that vectorization does not remove.
3. Two more byte-at-a-time passes over the same bytes that SIMD in nextAction does not touch, and that the plan's invariants fence off:
   - Terminal.swift:7672-7677 -- a continuation-byte counting scan (`if bytes[scan] & 0xC0 != 0x80 { scalarCount += 1 }`), bounded by `scalarCount < columnCount`.
   - Terminal.swift:7679-7690 -- a SECOND full DFA decode with a fresh `var decoder = UTF8Decoder()` inside a `(Int) -> Unicode.Scalar` closure handed to printBulkNarrow. Plan invariant I6 states this explicitly ("each admitted scalar is decoded twice by construction"); RI2 rejects carrying scalars in the action; I4 forbids "per-run scratch collection of scalars or offsets ... materialized on the feed path", which is exactly what a block decoder wants for the reducer side.
   Net: nextAction is ~1 of 3 passes over this byte range.
4. Simpler wins first, no SIMD needed. UTF8Decoder.characterClasses / transitions are `private static let [UInt8]`: every byte pays 2 swift_once-guarded global addressor calls + 2 release-mode Array bounds checks + 2 loads, and that is paid TWICE per byte because of the double decode. InlineArray (Swift 6.3 toolchain per F16) or a static blob helps both passes. Packing isBulkPrintable into a bitmask over the 29-entry palette replaces a struct load + 5 comparisons with a shift-and-test. The continuation-count scan is the one trivially SIMD-able piece and today defeats auto-vectorization only because of its columnCount early exit -- restructurable as a bounded popcount with no explicit SIMD at all.

Contrary to the finder's "no published profile covers it": the plan's own Implementation notes report an attribution sample on styled-screen-redraw with Terminal.printBulkNarrow at 18.9% self and TerminalInputStream.nextAction at 8.1% self (16,660 samples). That corpus is 0% non-ASCII so it does not measure this loop, but it bounds nextAction's total share at ~8%, of which the DFA is a fraction. The plan's AR3 also records that a Unicode-confined effect is diluted by the aggregate terminal-feed verdict, so the committed gate is unlikely to resolve this either way.

verified.title: appendCells: the per-cell admission encode loop
verified.simd_shape: Process the buffer in blocks of 4-8 cells. Source is POD stride 16, so a block is SIMD8<UInt64> loaded from the raw pointer; even lanes are cell words, odd lanes are (contentIdentity | hyperlinkId<<32). (1) `contentUnits`: `k = (words >> 21) & 7`, count lanes where `k != 3 && k != 4` -- one vector compare plus a mask popcount instead of a switch per cell. (2) Spill/wide-head detection: one `.&` against the spill bit and one `.==` against kind 2 over the whole block; the scalar fallback only runs for a block where either mask is nonzero. (3) The word store is a stride-16 -> stride-8 deinterleave (NEON `uzp1`), written through `chunk.withUnsafeMutableBufferPointer` so the per-element bounds check the comment already names disappears. (4) The identity-run extension is the real win: instead of unwrapping `openPreviousIdentity`, reading `openIdentityRuns.last` and doing an array modify per cell, check with one SIMD compare that the block's odd-lane low halves equal `base + iota`, and if so extend the open run by the whole block at once. `writeNarrowCells` (Terminal.swift:7849) stamps a strictly incrementing identity on every printed ASCII cell, so this is the common case, not a special case.
verified.hot_path_evidence: research/33/F42 (findings.md:3444-3447), profile `.build/terminal-feed-profiles/2026-08-09-193015`, 12,087 weighted samples on `scrollback-stream` at HEAD 5a8fb12b: `LogicalLineStore.appendCells` is 22.60% inclusive and 15.29% self. verified.risks: The loop is not a pure map: it mutates four pieces of open-record scratch (`openSpills`, `openHyperlinks`, `openIdentityRuns`, `openPreviousIdentity`) and calls an arbitrary `resolveSpill` closure. A block-at-a-time rewrite must keep the exact ordering of spill indices and run boundaries or retained content decodes wrong -- and a wrong identity run is invisible until a selection or search reads it. The existing `swap(&chunk, &chunks[chunkAt])` dance has a stated invariant ("Nothing between the two swaps may read the arena") that a `withUnsafeMutableBufferPointer` nesting must not break. Escape hatch: the deinterleave and the bounds-check removal can land alone, without the classification vectors, and be measured separately.

confidence_review.verdict:
Feasible, but not trivially so, and largely pre-empted by a plain scalar rewrite. The mechanical preconditions for SIMD are genuinely met — better than the finder even argues — but the loop carries four order-dependent scratch mutations that force a two-path (vector fast block + scalar fallback) structure, and the cheap scalar version of the same idea captures most of the win with none of the risk. The "high impact" claim rests on a profile that predates the commit which removed the expensive part of this loop.

WHAT SURVIVES (the vectorization preconditions are real):
- Source is already `UnsafeBufferPointer<Terminal.GridCell>` (LogicalLineStore.swift:2893-2896). No CoW, no Array indexing, no bounds checks on the read side in release.
- `GridCell` is POD with a 16-byte stride, asserted by a test (`Terminal.isGridCellTriviallyCopyable`, `gridCellStrideBytes == 16`, TerminalCellRepresentationTests.swift:11-15). Confirmed.
- No resumability, UTF-8, grapheme, or error-replacement semantics anywhere near this loop. Cells arrive fully decoded; scalars are already packed into bits 0..20 of the word or spilled.
- No chunk-boundary hazard, which the finder didn't claim but which is the thing that would have killed it: `makeRoom(forCells: cellCount + pendingMarginCapacity)` runs before `openRecordIfNeeded` (LogicalLineStore.swift:768-769), and the loop's own comment cites `research/31/D5` — "the record's cells are one run inside one backing chunk". A block of 8 can never straddle two chunks.
- The classification IS a clean vector compare. `TerminalCellKind.packedCode` is padding=0, narrow=1, wideHead=2, wideTail=3, spacerHead=4 (LogicalLineRecord.swift:457-465), so `contentUnits` is exactly "count lanes where `(w >> 21) & 7 < 3`" — one compare plus a mask popcount.
- The identity fast path is the common case, as claimed. `writeNarrowCells` (Terminal.swift:7844-7860) stamps `contentIdentity: baseIdentity + ContentIdentity(offset)` on every printed narrow cell, and `nextContentIdentity` keeps incrementing across print calls, so a whole admitted row is normally one run.

WHAT BLOCKS IT:
- Four loop-carried, order-dependent mutations: `openSpills.count` feeds the encoded word of the *next* spilled cell; `openHyperlinks.append` and `openIdentityRuns` are ordered appends; `openPreviousIdentity` is a rolling scalar. Auto-vectorization is impossible here — no vectorizer touches this — so explicit SIMD means writing the scalar loop twice (block fast path plus per-cell fallback) over an intricate encoder. The finder names this risk honestly, and it's the right risk.
- The odd-lane load is dirtier than described (see corrections): bytes 14..15 of each cell are padding, so the "identity | hyperlink" lane has 16 bits of uninitialized memory that every compare must mask off.
- The block fast path's entry condition is subtle: extending the open run requires BOTH `identity == previous &+ 1` AND `open.start + open.extent == cellOffset` (LogicalLineStore.swift:2957-2958). The run can be open from a previous `appendCells` call or from `loadOpenScratch` reopening a closed record (line 3068-3093), so the block check must reproduce that entry state exactly. A wrong run is silently wrong until a selection or search reads it back through the binary search at line 2765.

WHY A SCALAR REWRITE PRE-EMPTS IT: three changes, all obviously correct, remove most of the per-cell overhead before any SIMD:
1. `chunk.withUnsafeMutableBufferPointer` around the store — removes a per-element ContiguousArray bounds check AND a per-element uniqueness check.
2. Hoist `openIdentityRuns.last` into a local `var` for the loop, write back once — removes an Optional-returning bounds-checked `last` read plus a modify-subscript (uniqueness + bounds again) on every single printed cell. This is the finder's "real win," and it needs no vectors.
3. Hoist `originalCellOffset` (it is a loop-invariant base plus index, LogicalLineStore.swift:2640-2648) and read the kind bits raw instead of `cells[index].kind`, which builds a `TerminalCellKind` enum through a switch (LogicalLineRecord.swift:316) only for the loop to switch on it again.

Per the project's measurement discipline, you land that, measure, and quite possibly find the residual doesn't justify a two-path SIMD encoder.

confidence_review.evidence:
SEMANTICS (favor the candidate). admissionExtent is a pure per-row read with no cross-call state: no resumability, no chunk boundaries, no maximal-subpart replacement, no grapheme clustering. The whole content decision is 3 bits of each cell word. TerminalCellKind.packedCode (lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/LogicalLineRecord.swift:457) is padding 0, narrow 1, wideHead 2, wideTail 3, spacerHead 4, so masking k to 3 bits and testing `(k &- 1) & ~1 == 0` selects exactly {narrow, wideHead}. Wide-head width and the `min(width, column + 2)` clamp are a scalar fixup inside the single block that carries the highest set lane -- exact, not approximated. The second (fill) loop at LogicalLineStore.swift:838-848 is short, style-comparing, and stays scalar with no interaction. So the "is it compatible with block-wise processing" half of the lens is a pass.

LAYOUT (refutes the stated shape). GridCell (Terminal.swift:209) is `word: CellWord` (UInt64) + ContentIdentity (UInt32) + HyperlinkId (UInt16, Terminal.swift:183) -- 14 bytes of fields, 16-byte stride, pinned by TerminalMemoryCensusTests.swift:319 (`census.cellStrideBytes == 16`). The cell words are therefore NOT contiguous UInt64s: reinterpreting `[GridCell]` as UInt64 gives word at even lanes and (identity|hyperlink|2 bytes tail padding) at odd lanes. A SIMD8<UInt64> load covers 4 cells, not 8, and half of every vector register is junk that must be masked off. On ARM64 that is 4 cells per 4 NEON registers -- roughly a 2x ceiling over a tight scalar loop, not the 4-8x the shape implies. The candidate's "blocks of 4-8 cells reinterpreted as UInt64 lanes" is off by 2x.

The "cheaper first cut" is unsound as written. A default-blank cell's *word* is zero (padding packs to 0, Terminal.defaultStyleId == 0, Terminal.swift:1083), but the cell's 16 bytes are not provably zero: bytes 14-15 are struct tail padding whose contents Swift does not define, and a zero-word cell can legitimately carry a nonzero hyperlinkId or contentIdentity (GridCell's ids are independent of the word). So a raw 16-byte `.== .zero` can report "content" on a blank cell. You must mask to the even/word lanes -- at which point the zero test costs the same as the kind test and buys nothing extra. Also note the fast path degenerates whenever the tail was painted by a background erase: the fill blank's word is nonzero (styleId != 0) while its kind is still .padding, so on a colored-erase corpus only the kind decode survives.

Swift also does not guarantee this struct layout (CellWord/GridCell are not @frozen and carry no C layout attribute), so the reinterpretation needs withMemoryRebound over an assumed field order. It works today and the stride test would catch a shape change, but nothing else in the tree makes a layout assumption like it.

CoW / BOUNDS CHECKS. `admit(_ row: Terminal.GridRow)` takes the row by value and admissionExtent only reads it, so `row.cells.withUnsafeBufferPointer` is safe and triggers no CoW. That much of the pitch is right: the loop today is a bare Array subscript, so it does pay a bounds check per iteration.

AUTO-VECTORIZATION IS OFF THE TABLE, which cuts both ways. This is a reverse search with a data-dependent `break`; LLVM will not speculate loads past the exit condition, so removing bounds checks alone will not vectorize it. That kills the "just rewrite for auto-vectorization" option -- but it also means explicit SIMD must beat a *tightened scalar* loop, not today's loop.

THE SCALAR REWRITE PROBABLY CAPTURES MOST OF IT. Today each iteration pays: a bounds check, a 16-byte-strided load, a shift/mask, and a round trip through `TerminalCellKind(packedCode:)` -- a 5-case switch with a default that folds 0/5/6/7 to .padding -- before comparing against two enum cases. Replacing that with a `while` over an UnsafeBufferPointer testing `(cell.word.raw >> 21) & 7` directly (and short-circuiting on `raw == 0` for never-written tails) is 3-4 instructions per cell with no layout assumption at all. In-tree precedent: research/28 F20 Observation 2 (docs/research/28-retained-row-optimizations/findings.md:2275) already adopted exactly the "a never-written cell encodes to a zero word, so the writer skips it" trick in `pack`.

MAGNITUDE, which bounds how much feasibility is worth. research/33 F16/F17 (docs/research/33-by-construction-perf-survey/findings.md:1307, :1410) put the current scrollback-stream drain at ~70-83 ms after the bulk-ASCII-run work; the same doc (:444) gives a mean line length of 60 at 179 columns, so the scan is ~119 tail cells x 25,000 rows ~= 3.0M iterations. At even 2-3 cycles per iteration on a descending, cache-friendly stream that is ~2-3 ms, i.e. low single digits of the block, against a scrollback-stream freeze threshold of 1.85% (findings.md:1187). A SIMD version that captures half of a ~3% loop is at or below the instrument's resolution.

CORRECT AND USEFUL IN THE PITCH: the risk section is honest (demands attribution before building), and it names the right ideal. That ideal is stronger than stated -- a maintained contentEnd on GridRow also retires Terminal.retainedContentEnd(in:) (Terminal.swift:6376), which is the identical reverse scan spelled with lastIndex(where:) and is called from the trailing-blank-row trim at Terminal.swift:2247 and from the projections at :3153/:3208.

Filling the padding too makes it one: build the 16-byte pattern once (`SIMD2<UInt64>(word.raw, UInt64(identity) | UInt64(hyperlink) << 32)`, both zero for a blank) and store it per element through `UnsafeMutableRawBufferPointer`, or call `memset_pattern16` over `UnsafeMutableRawBufferPointer(rebasing:)` directly. verified.simd_shape: Every field except the scalar and the identity is loop-invariant, and both varying fields are affine. REFUTATION 1 - a scalar rewrite gets most of it, no SIMD.
Per cell the loop currently pays, beyond the store: construction of `TerminalScalars.single(...)`, whose `Storage` has a `.spill([Unicode.Scalar])` case (TerminalScalars.swift:39) and so is non-POD; a `scalars.first.map { } ?? ` optional dance; and three `precondition`s that are live at `-O` (`scalars.count <= 1`, `hyperlinkId != 0`, `contentIdentity != 0`, Terminal.swift:216-218). Hoisting `head` and calling that leaves one OR plus one 16-byte store per cell. That is the cheap capture, and it is also the prerequisite for anything vectorized, because the preconditions are branches the vectorizer will not cross.

REFUTATION 2 - the proposed SIMD shape is not expressible in Swift, and is weak on arm64.
`UInt64` lanes give 2 per 128-bit register, so `SIMD4<UInt64>` is 2 registers and the described 4-cell block is 4. The interleave the candidate names (`zip1`/`zip2` -> `st2`) has no stdlib SIMD API; Swift exposes no shuffle. Building a `SIMD8<UInt64>` element-wise typically round-trips a stack temp, which is slower than the scalar stores it replaces. The realistic route is LLVM's interleaved-access group (factor 2) via *auto*-vectorization, i.e. exactly refutation 1's cleanup, not hand SIMD. Every member is trivial, so the type is POD at stride 16 and `memmove` is legal. `UnsafeMutableBufferPointer`'s subscript bounds check is `_debugPrecondition`, so it is already absent in release. Nothing blocks the rewrite.

PERMUTATION — a clean contiguous shift. All four call sites pass `screen.cursor.column..<columnCount` (Terminal.swift:8241, 8304, 8456, 8466), i.e. always a suffix of the row; there is no left/right-margin variant. `moveInPlace` (8519) clips the source to `range`, so for `delta > 0` the map is dest `[lo+amount, hi)` <- src `[lo, hi-amount)` with vacated `[lo, lo+amount)`, and the mirror for `delta < 0`. `amount = min(abs(delta), range.count)` means the degenerate all-vacated case is `movedCount == 0`. That is exactly one `memmove` of `(range.count - amount) * 16` bytes plus one `update(repeating: blank)` over the vacated strip. No edge case survives.

Multi-scalar cells are safe because `GridRow.spills` is per-row and the shift never leaves the row, so a byte-identical word keeps a valid `spillIndex` (LogicalLineRecord CellWord `spillBit`/`spillIndex`; GridRow.scalars(of:) at Terminal.swift:~305). So a real (if small) constant-factor win exists: roughly a two-compare + branch + Optional per 16-byte copy, replaced by libc's vectorized copy.

A SIMD compare would have to load and compare a full vector before it could bail, making the common case slower, not faster. Vectorizing a loop whose expected trip count is 1 has no win to capture regardless of layout.

verified.title: Style-id run-boundary scan over the retained arena's contiguous UInt64 cell words
verified.simd_shape: The scan is `find the first index >= start whose (word >> 32) differs from a splat`. Inside `withPaintedCells` the pointer is already in hand, so a store-side primitive -- `func styleRunEnd(from:limit:) -> Int` or, better, a segment emitter that hands the caller `(Range<Int>, StyleId)` pairs -- can do: load `SIMD4<UInt64>` (or SIMD8) from `words.baseAddress! + cellsBase + shape.start + column`, `>> 32`, `.!= SIMD4(repeating: styleId)`, then `mask.firstIndex(where:)` / `simd_any` to locate the boundary word, scalar-refine inside the vector. verified.hot_path_evidence: research/33/F32 (docs/research/33-by-construction-perf-survey/findings.md:2914-2946): one canonical 179x66 `planFrame` visits 11,814 cells and observes exactly 66 distinct style runs -- i.e. the average run is a full row, so this loop walks ~179 columns per boundary it finds. verified.title: Per-cell ink-class ASCII range test folded into a row-level OR reduction
verified.simd_shape: This is a pure OR-reduction with no loop-carried dependency and no early exit -- the textbook auto-vectorizable shape, and trivially hand-vectorizable. Over the retained arena it reduces to word math: for a `SIMD4<UInt64>` of cell words, `isSpilled = raw & (1<<24)`, `payload = raw & 0x1F_FFFF`, `ascii = (payload &- 0x20) .< 0x5F`, OR the three class masks across lanes and reduce once per row. It is only reachable as SIMD if the ink class is computed inside `TerminalCore` from the arena words rather than accumulated one closure-delivered `TerminalScalars` at a time in `TerminalRenderPlanning`.
verified.hot_path_evidence: None directly. The class feeds `renderRowReaches` (RenderInkReach.swift:78-88), added by research/33 T14/D9; no profile in docs/research/ attributes time to the classification itself. It rides the same per-cell visit that research/17's `forEachViewportCell` row covers (1.19 / 4.00 / 3.82 / 0.89 %).
verified.risks: The win is a few thousand compares per frame that the branch predictor already handles almost free, and the reduction is not the cost -- the surrounding `RenderTextCell` construction and open-run continuation checks are. 2. THE DATA IS NOT UNIFORMLY CONTIGUOUS. Two row sources feed the planner from `Terminal.forEachViewportRow` (Terminal.swift:5121):

verified.title: Per-device-pixel sin() sampling in strokeCurlyUnderline
verified.simd_shape: One libm `sin` call per backing pixel of the run's width (a full-width run at 179 columns on a 2x display is ~2,800 samples). Uniform math over a contiguous index range, no data dependency: fill a `[Double]` of phases and call `vvsin` / `vDSP` once, or use `SIMD4<Double>` with a polynomial approximation. The honest better fix is not SIMD at all: the wave has period `max(cellWidth, 4*deviceStep)`, so one period's y-samples can be precomputed once per metrics change and indexed modulo the period, removing every `sin` call rather than vectorizing them.

verified.title: Per-cell classification and glyph emission in drawTextRuns

confidence_review.verdict: REFUTED on feasibility. This is not a loop that can be vectorized; it is a multi-sink scatter-emission loop whose measured cost lives in Array append traffic and ARC, both of which the existing lead ledger already names as scalar fixes (18/L4, 18/L13). The candidate's own admission that data_layout_ready=false understates the problem: making it ready is a public cross-target representation change to an Equatable value type, and even after that change the body would still be scalar.
confidence_review.evidence:
Code read at lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalRenderExecution/TerminalRenderExecution.swift:951 (`for cell in run.cells`, inside `for run in row.textRuns` at :917), plus TerminalRenderPlanning.swift:379-420 and TerminalCore/TerminalScalars.swift.

1. No contiguous scalar buffer exists, and the element type forbids a vector load. `run.cells` is `[RenderTextCell]`; `RenderTextCell` is `{ scalars: TerminalScalars, columnWidth: Int }` (TerminalRenderPlanning.swift:379-389). `TerminalScalars` wraps `enum Storage { empty / single(Unicode.Scalar) / spill([Unicode.Scalar]) }` (TerminalScalars.swift:39-43), so the element is non-POD with a refcounted case. `withUnsafeBufferPointer` on `run.cells` yields a pointer to non-trivial structs at a stride, not to UInt32 lanes. Gathering the scalar field into a SIMD8<UInt32> is itself a scalar strided-load loop -- and arm64 has no vector gather instruction -- so the gather costs more than the compare it feeds.

2. The proposed fix is a representation change across a public seam, not a loop rewrite. `RenderTextRun`/`RenderTextCell` are `public`, `Equatable`, `Sendable`, and the whole frame plan is compared by value. Adding parallel `[UInt32]`/`[UInt8]`/spill-mask columns either changes what plan equality means or creates a second authority for cell payload. It also moves append traffic into `RenderFramePlanner.swift:480`, which is itself on the hot path -- paying planner-side Array growth to save executor-side `cmp`.

3. The body cannot be block-processed even with ideal layout. Per iteration the loop appends into twelve different variable-length sinks: `mappedGlyphs`+`positions`, `characters`+`candidateCells`, `fallbackCells`, `spriteRects`, `shadedSpriteRects[shade]`, `geometricShapeTriangles`, `powerlinePaths`, `branchDrawingGeometries`, `legacySpriteRects[alpha]`, `boxDrawingStrokes`. A SIMD mask only tells you which lanes go where; turning a mask into compacted output needs a compress-store, which NEON/Swift SIMD does not have. You get mask -> bitmask -> ctz -> per-lane scalar append, i.e. the same scalar work plus vector prologue and epilogue.

4. The claimed win is a single predicted instruction. The reject test is already one compare against a constant (`scalar.value >= spriteClassificationMinimumScalar`, defined 0x2500 at :749), and the `column` walk is one integer add of a 1-or-2 width. Both are latency-1 and fully hidden behind the append and the `glyphs[value - 0x20]` table load in `TerminalFace.asciiGlyph` (:347-350).

5. Measured run lengths defeat the vector width. research/11/F8: twelve committed streams from DanTerm's corpus and alacritty session recordings run 5.8 to 66.6 cells per run. At the low end (heavily-colored btop-shaped output, which is exactly the churn workload this candidate is priced on) a run is shorter than one SIMD8 group, so the sweep is all prologue/tail.

6. A non-SIMD rewrite already captures the real cost, and it is already ranked. research/18's lead table: `L4` -- replace per-element `Array.append` in this run loop with writes into pre-sized unsafe buffers -- is "confirmed and measured at 24.5% of the live bracket" and was promoted to tier 1; `L13` -- borrow rather than copy `TerminalScalars.Storage` in this exact classification loop -- is 3.4%. By contrast research/18/F12's owner partition puts "our own Swift loop bodies (L3, L13, classification)" at 88 ms / 8.2% (content-churn) of a 1,075 ms bracket, and classification is only a fraction of that shared bucket. So the array traffic is ~3x everything the SIMD proposal touches, and it is fixed with UnsafeMutableBufferPointer, not lanes.

7. The one point in the candidate's favor: there is no resumability, chunk-boundary, or UTF-8 replacement hazard here. Each run is fully materialized before the loop, wide cells are a plain 1-or-2 width, and grapheme clusters are already routed out via `cell.scalars.count == 1`. Semantics are block-compatible. That is why this scores 1 rather than 0 -- the obstacle is purely layout, dispatch shape, and worthlessness of the win, not correctness.

8. Measurement ceiling confirms it is undecidable anyway. research/33/F26: post-T25 `drawRenderFrame` is 6.25 s of 10.60 s process CPU on content-churn, but memset_pattern16 is 3.62 s and glyph colorize/blit 1.33 + 1.51 s -- rasterization, not our loop. The Swift loop bodies did not grow; the denominator did.

confidence_review.evidence:
1. THE INDEX MAP IS NOT AFFINE. In `drawTextRuns` (lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalRenderExecution/TerminalRenderExecution.swift:986-1093) the loop is `for cell in run.cells` with `column += cell.columnWidth` at :1092. An entry reaches `positions` only when the cell is not a sprite AND `face.asciiGlyph(scalar.value)` returns non-nil AND that glyph is non-zero (:1076-1085). Everything else consumes a column and appends nothing: sprite families append to `spriteRects`/`boxDrawingStrokes`/etc., `glyph == 0` goes to `fallbackCells`, unmapped scalars go to `candidateCells`, and `columnWidth == 2` skips a column outright. So position index i does NOT map to `run.startColumn + i`. `vDSP_vrampD` can only produce the columns after a scalar pass has already produced the accepted-column list -- and that pass is the loop you were trying to replace.

2. THE SECOND SITE IS A GATHER BY CONSTRUCTION. :1157-1169 appends the batched-cmap residue into the SAME `positions` array after the cell loop finishes, taking `candidate.column` out of a `[(cell: RenderTextCell, column: Int)]` tuple array, and skipping entries where `glyph == 0` (:1147-1156). The final array is therefore "ASCII columns in order, then residue columns in order" -- two interleaved subsequences, neither dense. `vDSP_vrampD` has no shape here at all.

3. NO ARITHMETIC TO SAVE. `glyphOrigin` (:776-786) is `x = CGFloat(column) * cellSize.width` and `y = -(CGFloat(row) * cellSize.height + baselineOffset)`. `y` is constant for the whole run and LLVM already hoists it; `x` is one multiply. The candidate's own `simd_shape` names the real target -- "the per-element uniqueness check and capacity test that `Array.append` emits" -- which is CoW traffic, not instruction width. Widening stores does not remove `swift_isUniquelyReferenced_nonNull_native`; only writing through a pointer does, and that is L4, not SIMD.

4. THE API BLOCKS THE OVER-SIZED BUFFER. research/18 F15: `CGContextShowGlyphsAtPositions` is `unavailable` in Swift ("Use showGlyphs(_:at:)"), and `showGlyphs` takes `[CGGlyph]` and `[CGPoint]` with NO count parameter -- it derives the count from `Array.count`. Confirmed at the call site (:1188: `showGlyphs(mappedGlyphs, at: positions)`). An over-sized vector-filled buffer draws its stale tail. So any pointer/SIMD fill must be scratch-plus-copy into an exact-count `Array`, and F15 measured that copy: `_platform_memmove` in the bracket GREW 58 ms -> 76 ms.

5. SAFE ALTERNATIVES DO NOT CAPTURE IT EITHER. `memset`/`initialize(repeating:)` is inapplicable -- every element differs. `reserveCapacity` after the `removeAll(keepingCapacity: true)` sweep (:922-935) removes reallocation but not the per-append uniqueness check, which was the 88 ms leaf. `Array(unsafeUninitializedCapacity:)` would give an exact-count array with no memmove, but it needs the accepted-glyph count up front, which is only known after classification -- so it degenerates to F15's scratch-plus-copy with a marginally nicer final step. Auto-vectorization is out: the loop body is a switch over eight sprite coarse ranges plus a `TerminalScalars` enum discriminant (`.empty`/`.single`/`.spill`, TerminalScalars.swift:39-43), i.e. unpredictable control flow and a heap-spill case per element.

Reachable share was ~15% of the bracket, delivered ~5x less. impact_review.corrections:
Three factual corrections to the candidate, none of which change the score:

1. Sample count is understated, and it is per-run, not per-row. `deviceStep = 1/displayScale`, and the loop spans `runRect.minX/deviceStep` to `runRect.maxX/deviceStep` (plus one sample on each side), so the count is the run's width in *device pixels*, i.e. width_points x displayScale. A full-width 179-column row is ~1300-1500pt, which is ~2600-3000 samples at 2x, not ~1600. But it is bounded by the *run* rect, and a curly-underlined run is normally a few words, so real-world counts are tens to low hundreds.

2. The "hoist one period" alternative is not exactly correct as stated. `x` is absolute (`CGFloat(sample) * deviceStep` from the context origin, not run-relative), and the wave period is `max(metrics.cellSize.width, deviceStep * 4)` in points. The sample lattice repeats per cell only if `cellSize.width * displayScale` is an integer, which it generally is not for a fractional advance width. The hoist would need a phase-indexed table (or accepting a sub-pixel phase error), not a straight copy of one cell's samples. The idea is still the better fix than SIMD -- it just needs that caveat.

3. The guard block (:1558-1570) rejects negative or non-finite bounds and overflow, so `firstSample...lastSample` is always a valid non-empty range -- worth noting because a naive Accelerate rewrite over a pre-sized buffer would have to preserve those early returns.

The candidate's core risk claim is right and is the decisive one: `CGMutablePath.addLine` per sample plus `strokePath()` on an antialiased n-segment polyline is the dominant term, and vectorizing `sin` leaves it untouched.

confidence_review.verdict: Confirmed as a non-candidate, and the refutation is stronger than the finder states. Worse for the SIMD case: the sine sequence here is *exactly periodic in the integer sample index*, so a ~16-entry lookup table computed once per metrics eliminates 100% of the transcendental work with no vector code, no Accelerate dependency, and bit-identical output. Explicit SIMD is strictly dominated by the trivial scalar fix, and both are dominated by CoreGraphics rasterizing a multi-thousand-segment antialiased polyline. No perf-ladder workload exercises the path at all.

Loop confirmed verbatim at /Users/dan/Code/danterm/lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalRenderExecution/TerminalRenderExecution.swift:1553-1592 (`strokeCurlyUnderline`), sole call site at line 1500 inside `drawDecorationRuns` (line 1458), itself called once per frame from line 668 over the damaged-row selection.

Exact periodicity proof (the finder's "hoist" idea is not just plausible, it is provably exact): `TerminalRenderMetrics.cellSize` is built at line 171 as `width: CGFloat(cellWidthPixels) / displayScale`, where `cellWidthPixels` comes from `quantizedPixelCount` (line 675) which returns an Int only when `CGFloat(pixels) == rounded` exactly. So `period / deviceStep == cellWidthPixels` exactly, and when the `max(..., deviceStep * 4)` clamp at line 1556 fires, it is exactly 4. Therefore `sin(2 * .pi * x / period) == sin(2 * .pi * Double(sample) / Double(n))` with integer n, i.e. the value depends only on `sample mod n`. A cached `[Double]` of n entries (typically 8-24 at 2x) replaces every `sin` call. One caveat the finder does not mention: `firstSample` is `Int(firstValue) - 1` (line 1568-1571) and `firstValue >= 0` is only guarded to be non-negative, so `sample` can be -1 and the index must be `((sample % n) + n) % n`.

Vectorization mechanics, against the lens criteria:
- Contiguity: there is no existing contiguous buffer. A vvsin approach must *synthesize* a ramp into a fresh `[Double]`, call vvsin, then interleave into CGPoints -- three passes plus an allocation replacing one fused loop.
- Consumer blocks it: `path.addLine(to:)` per sample is a CoreGraphics C call. The only batching lever is `CGMutablePath.addLines(between: [CGPoint])`, which forces an Array materialization per run (allocation on every curly run, no CoW sharing possible since the contents differ per run).
- Auto-vectorization: irrelevant here -- LLVM cannot vectorize across the opaque `addLine` call, and it will not vectorize libm `sin` without a vector math library.
- The dominant term is unchanged: `strokePath()` (line 1591) rasterizing an n-thousand-segment antialiased polyline into the CG backing store.

Hot-path evidence: confirmed absent. Grepping docs/research, scripts/, and lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalDrawBenchmarkSupport for `curly|undercurl|4:3` returns no benchmark or profile hit. The one hit outside the renderer is /Users/dan/Code/danterm/scripts/import-alacritty-recordings.py:125, mapping Alacritty's `UNDERCURL` flag to a `"curly"` *correctness* fixture -- so the path has conformance coverage but zero perf coverage.
confidence_review.corrections:
1. Sample-count arithmetic is off. The loop runs per decoration *run*, not per row, and emits `runWidthPixels + 3` samples. With `cellWidthPixels` typically 15-17 at 2x, a full 179-column run is ~2,700-3,000 samples, not ~1,600. Direction is right; the number is low by roughly half.

2. The "hoist it entirely" alternative is undersold as a maybe. It is exactly correct and bit-identical, guaranteed by `cellSize.width == CGFloat(cellWidthPixels) / displayScale` (line 171). The finder should have stated it as the answer rather than "a better fix than SIMD if this ever matters" -- it is a ~10-line change that removes the entire transcendental chain, and the SIMD option should be dropped outright, not merely deprioritized.

3. "No workload emits SGR 4:3" is right for the perf ladder but reads as "untested". The path has correctness fixtures imported from Alacritty recordings (UNDERCURL -> "curly"). The gap is benchmark coverage only.

4. `data_layout_ready: false` is correct but for a reason not given: the issue is not that a buffer needs reshaping, it is that no buffer exists -- the input is a synthesized integer ramp and the output sink is a serial CG path API.

5. Minor: the sibling `fillPatternedUnderline` (line 1524) has the same per-pixel-ish structure (one `fill` per dash period) and was not mentioned; it is equally not worth vectorizing, and equally has no profile evidence, but if anyone ever touches decoration cost it is the same family of work.

verified.title: Own the glyph raster: SIMD mask-colorize blit instead of CoreGraphics glyph submission
verified.simd_shape: Rasterize each (glyph, face) once into an owned 8-bit coverage atlas, then blit into the IOSurface ourselves: per 16 destination pixels, load `SIMD16<UInt8>` of mask, widen to two `SIMD8<UInt16>`, lerp between the run foreground and the already-filled background per channel, narrow, and store four `SIMD4<UInt8>` BGRA quads. The destination is ready for this today -- `TerminalFrameBackingStore` already holds `private let data: UnsafeMutableRawPointer` (:42) over a BGRA8888 IOSurface with a known `bytesPerRow` (:40), and glyph origins are integral in device pixels by construction (research/30/F10: metrics quantize to whole device pixels and then divide by scale).
verified.hot_path_evidence: research/33/F26, the largest pixel-level CPU in the whole process post-T25: on content-churn, glyph colorize/blit is `CGSColorMaskCopyARGB8888` 1.33 s plus `RIPLayerBltGlyph` 1.51 s of a 10.60 s 20-second trace -- about 27% of process CPU -- against 0 s / 0.01 s on the pre-T25 baseline, because T25 moved rasterization from CoreAnimation's GPU display-list renderer into the app's own CPU account.
verified.risks: This is not a loop tweak; it is replacing CoreGraphics text rasterization with our own, which docs/research/18/F3 records as the road every fast terminal ultimately took (GPU glyph atlas) and which `09-renderer.md` explicitly deferred. Three specific reasons to doubt the win: (1) `CGSColorMaskCopyARGB8888` and `RIPLayerBltGlyph` are already hand-tuned NEON, so a hand-written blitter competes on overhead removal, not instruction width; (2) it does not delete the mask *generation* cost, only the colorize-and-blit; (3) it puts font rasterization fidelity -- antialiasing, gamma, hinting, `.copy` blend semantics -- under our own maintenance, and the byte-equality gate research/33/F27 relies on would have to be rewritten against a new ground truth. Also note research/17/F16: the churn workloads are frame-rate-capped, so this is CPU/energy, not throughput. If taken at all, the honest ideal is the GPU atlas, not a CPU SIMD blitter; the CPU version buys a fraction of the same win and keeps the raster on the main thread.

impact_review.verdict: Real and large on the profile, but concentrated in two of five ladder workloads and second-ranked even there. Post-T25 the glyph colorize/blit runs on the main thread inside the `drawNanosecondsPerDraw` bracket, so it is ~45% of the deciding metric's own bracket on content-churn/style-churn -- plausibly >5% end-to-end there if a hand-written blitter beats CoreGraphics by even ~15%. It is worth ~0% on terminal-feed and under ~1% on scrollback-stream. The residual risk is not "is it on the profile" (it is) but "can a Swift SIMD blitter beat already-NEON-tuned CG blit code", which no evidence in the tree addresses.
impact_review.evidence:
SITE CONFIRMED. /Users/dan/Code/danterm/lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalRenderExecution/TerminalRenderExecution.swift:1187-1196 is exactly the quoted `showGlyphs(mappedGlyphs, at: positions)` / `CTFontDrawGlyphs` pair, inside the per-run text loop that also handles symbols and fallback cells.

PROFILE WEIGHT. docs/research/33-by-construction-perf-survey/findings.md:2478 (F26), content-churn round 1, 20 s trace: `CGSColorMaskCopyARGB8888` 1.33 s + `RIPLayerBltGlyph` 1.51 s = 2.84 s of a 10.60 s whole-process total (26.8%), against 0 / 0.01 s pre-T25. Same table: main thread 9.71 s, render seam 7.47 s, `drawRenderFrame` 6.25 s. So the blit term is ~45% of `drawRenderFrame`, not 27% of the thing the benchmark actually decides on.

IT LANDS ON A CALIBRATED VERDICT. agent-docs/terminal-performance.md:114-135: the three serialized-draw workloads decide on `drawNanosecondsPerDraw`, "T25 moved this bracket ... The pane now rasterizes into its own IOSurface inside the bracket," and the post-move A/A screen "retained directional rules for `content-churn` and `style-churn`" while `incremental-mixed` is permanently uncalibratable. So the raster, glyph blit included, is inside the verdict metric of exactly two ladder workloads. THE OTHER THREE WORKLOADS ARE NEAR-ZERO. scripts/terminal-benchmark-compare.py:53-54 and :117-124: `terminal-feed` decides on `feedDurationNanoseconds` (parse path, no draw at all -> 0% here), and `scrollback-stream` has always been "~96% a PTY throughput measurement ... a change that touches only the draw path can move it by at most ~4%". Outside the benchmark's own draw-time number, the return is CPU/energy, not frames. The candidate states this correctly.

DATA LAYOUT CLAIM HOLDS, INDEPENDENTLY VERIFIED. TerminalFrameBackingStore.swift:36-42 has `private let bytesPerRow` and `private let data: UnsafeMutableRawPointer` over the BGRA IOSurface. Glyph origins are integral in device pixels: TerminalRenderExecution.swift:155-177 quantizes advance, line height AND ascent through `quantizedPixelCount` before dividing by `displayScale`, and glyphOrigin (:776-785) is `column * cellSize.width` / `row * cellSize.height + baselineOffset` -- all three terms pixel-integral. research/30/F10 (findings.md:458) states the same invariant for clip edges.
impact_review.corrections:

"the largest pixel-level CPU in the whole process post-T25" is wrong, and F26 says so in its own next-action line (findings.md:2530-2533 region): "background fills are one memset family at 34% of the process, ahead of any glyph cost." 2. "about 27% of process CPU" is arithmetically right but is the wrong denominator for impact. The benchmark verdict is `drawNanosecondsPerDraw`, a main-thread draw bracket; against `drawRenderFrame`'s 6.25 s the term is ~45%.
