confidence_review.verdict: The pixel kernel itself would vectorize cleanly -- but there is no Swift loop to vectorize today, and nothing in Swift is blocking one. The entire cost of this candidate is the prerequisite work (own rasterizer, own atlas, own clip, own color conversion) that must exist before a single SIMD16 lane is loaded. As a "vectorize a hot loop" item it is misfiled; as a "replace CoreGraphics text rasterization" item its confidence is correctly self-rated low. Feasible in principle, not cleanly vectorizable in the sense this lens asks about.
confidence_review.evidence:
Verified at /Users/dan/Code/danterm/lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalRenderExecution/TerminalRenderExecution.swift:1180-1194 (the cited submission) and the supporting files.

WHAT FAVORS IT (confirmed):
1. Integral device-pixel origins are real. `glyphOrigin` (:776-785) returns x = column * cellSize.width, y = -(row * cellSize.height + baselineOffset); the metrics init (:156-176) derives cellWidthPixels, cellHeightPixels and baselinePixels through `quantizedPixelCount(_:scale:)` and then divides by displayScale, so every glyph origin is a whole backing pixel after the CTM. A one-phase 8-bit atlas is therefore valid -- no subpixel-phase variants needed.
2. The destination is genuinely raw and contiguous. TerminalFrameBackingStore holds `private let data: UnsafeMutableRawPointer` (:41) over an IOSurface with a fixed `bytesPerRow` (:40), BGRA8888 premultipliedFirst byteOrder32Little (:87-92), top-left origin (:96-97). Rows are contiguous at a known stride; `translateRows` already does raw `memmove` over it (:229-233). No Array, no CoW, no bounds checks in the would-be inner loop.
3. Only one production destination. `drawRenderFrame` has exactly two production call sites, both TerminalFrameBackingStore (renderFull :130, apply :204); everything else is tests and the GlyphPreview tool.
4. No block-wise semantic hazards in the pixel loop. Ligatures are disabled (kCTLigatureAttributeName: 0, :1216), the batch path is per-cell single-BMP-scalar (surrogate pairs and multi-scalar clusters divert to `fallbackCells`, :1152-1163), and blending is lane-independent -- no resumability, chunk boundary, error-replacement, or grapheme concern reaches the blitter.

WHAT REFUTES IT (the feasibility cost):
5. There is no Swift loop here to vectorize. The "current_code" is two CoreGraphics submission calls. Nothing in Swift -- no bounds check, no CoW, no Array indexing -- is preventing vectorization; the pixels are inside CoreGraphics. So the SIMD kernel is the last few percent of a change whose bulk is writing a rasterizer, a per-(glyph, face, size) atlas and its eviction, and colorspace conversion.
6. The clip is the hard blocker. The incremental path (TerminalFrameBackingStore.apply :193-206) builds a multi-span, non-rectangular clip by `addRect` per erase span then `context.clip()`, and calls drawRenderFrame inside it; the test harness does the same (BitmapTestSupport.swift:242-260, :271-289). CGContext exposes only `boundingBoxOfClipPath` -- a raw blitter cannot read the span set, and honoring only the bbox would paint outside the erased spans, breaking exactly the byte-exactness F27/D9 was built to get. The clip must be lifted out of CGContext and threaded through drawRenderFrame's public signature as data. That is an API change through the whole executor, not a loop rewrite.
7. Two rasterizers, one frame. Sprites, box-drawing strokes, underlines, the symbols face (`drawPackagedSymbol`, :788) and the CTLine fallback (`drawTextCell`, :1219-1226) stay on CoreGraphics and use the same foreground color. Our blitter must match CG's AA/gamma/color-conversion numerically or the same color reads differently between a glyph and the box-drawing stroke beside it. The store is created with the window's colorspace (:63-67), so CG is doing a color conversion per fill that we would have to reproduce.
8. Blend is not a lerp. The surface is premultipliedFirst and is memset to 0 at init (:117); backgrounds are not guaranteed opaque, so the correct op is premultiplied src-over with a coverage mask, not "lerp between fg and bg". Cheap, but it is not the shape the candidate wrote.
9. `drawRenderFrame(_:metrics:in:)` is public and takes any CGContext. Owning the blit forces the destination to be a bitmap context of a known format (CGContext.data / bytesPerRow / bitmapInfo), or forces a second, CG-only path kept alive in parallel.

WHAT THE PROFILE ACTUALLY SUPPORTS: F26's ledger does imply the glyph cost is overhead-dominated, not bandwidth-dominated -- 2.84 s over ~2,100 frames at ~105 accepted draws/s is ~1.35 ms/frame for a few hundred to ~1,000 small masks, i.e. order nanoseconds per pixel, far above what NEON bandwidth would cost. So there is real overhead to remove. But that win comes from batching and deleting per-submission dispatch, not from instruction width -- SIMD is incidental to it.

CHEAPER LEVERS FIRST: the demonstrated lever in this tree has been submitting fewer glyphs over less area, not faster pixels -- F27 cut paced-scroll submission 1,086 -> 375 per frame by deriving the ink halo, with no fidelity risk and no new rasterizer. F26's own "next action" names background fills, already a `memset_pattern16` family (the optimal primitive; no SIMD headroom), as the larger term.
confidence_review.corrections:
1. "the largest pixel-level CPU in the whole process post-T25" is wrong. In the same F26 table, solid fills (`memset_pattern16` under `CGContextFillRect`) are 3.62 s against glyph colorize/blit's 1.33 + 1.51 = 2.84 s, and F26's closing line says so explicitly: "background fills are one memset family at 34% of the process, ahead of any glyph cost." The 27%-of-process arithmetic is right; the superlative is not.

2. "The destination is ready for this today" overstates. `data` is `private` to TerminalFrameBackingStore; the executor receives a `CGContext`, not the pointer, and would have to go through CGContext.data/bytesPerRow/bitmapInfo or take a new parameter. More importantly the destination is not the missing piece -- the clip is (point 6 above), and the candidate's risk list does not mention it at all.

3. The byte-equality risk is overstated in one direction and understated in another. The executor gates compare our incremental render against our own full render (BitmapTestSupport.renderBitmap vs renderIncrementalBitmap / renderDirtyRectBitmap, byte-comparing `Bitmap` values), not against a CoreText ground truth -- so a deterministic in-house rasterizer keeps those gates meaningful without "a new ground truth". What genuinely breaks is finer: those gates only stay honest if the blitter honors the same clip the CG path did, which is the unaddressed blocker.

4. research/30 F10 is "clip-rect edges are device-pixel aligned by construction", not the metrics-quantization finding. The integral-origin claim is true, but its evidence is TerminalRenderExecution.swift:156-176 plus :776-785, not 30/F10.

5. Minor: `mappedGlyphs`/`positions` are Swift Arrays, and the per-cell loop that fills them (:1147-1170) is Array-indexed with bounds checks -- but that loop is glyph mapping, not pixels, and is nowhere near the 2.84 s. No CoW or bounds-check problem exists on the path this candidate targets, which is itself part of why "vectorize" is the wrong frame for it.

rejected.title: EscapeAbsorber.consume state machine (ESC / CSI / DCS header states)
rejected.reason: Genuinely serial: every byte's handling depends on the state the previous byte left, and there is no run to amortize over -- a CSI is typically 3-10 bytes and `research/33/F10` counts CSI sequences per action, not in bulk. `research/10/F6` puts the whole of `consume` at 3.4-6.0%, and doc 10's folded stack attributes 222 of 256 of those samples to `dispatchCSI` rather than to byte stepping. Nothing to vectorize.

rejected.title: colonSeparators.allSatisfy { $0 == false } in dispatchCSI
rejected.reason: Looks like a scan and is not one: `CSIColonSeparators` (EscapeAbsorber.swift:150-190) already stores the flags as a `UInt32` bitmask, so the whole predicate is `bits == 0`. As written it iterates up to 24 elements through a subscript carrying a live `precondition(indices.contains(index))`. Worth fixing as a one-line bitmask read -- not a SIMD candidate, and short-circuited for SGR (`final == 0x6D`) anyway, which is the common CSI on style-churn.

rejected.title: collectParameter digit accumulation and CSIParameters/SequenceIntermediates packing
rejected.reason: Bounded at 24 parameters and 4 intermediates by construction (`CSIParameters.capacity`, `SequenceIntermediates` packs into one UInt32), and the accumulation is a serial multiply-add chain with overflow saturation. A vectorized digit parse needs a run of digits per parameter; real SGR parameters are 1-3 digits.

rejected.title: OSCPayload.decodeBase64 and appendDecodedBase64Quartet
rejected.reason: The textbook SIMD target, and still not worth it here. It runs once per OSC 52 clipboard write, is capped by the caller's `maximumByteCount`, appears in no benchmark workload and no research profile, and operates on an `ArraySlice<UInt8>` with no raw pointer. The strict quartet validation (`=` padding position, residual-bit checks, early `return nil`) is also exactly the part a vector decoder has to fall out of.

rejected.title: OSCPayload.percentDecoded / parseOSCSelector / progressPercent / canonicalExitStatus / normalizedHost
rejected.reason: All operate on OSC parameter fields of tens of bytes -- a selector, a percentage, a hostname, a file:// path -- once per OSC dispatch. `normalizedHost`'s ASCII-lowercase loop (line 199-201) is SIMD-shaped in the abstract and runs over a hostname. Below any measurement threshold.

rejected.title: Terminal.dispatchOSC payload splitting and OSC 133 option parsing
rejected.reason: `payload.firstIndex(of: 0x3B)` and the option walks run once per OSC, on payloads of tens of bytes, at shell-prompt frequency. `research/24` records these marks as emitted a handful of times per command, not per byte.

rejected.title: PTY read/drain path (takeOutputTurn, finishOutputTurn, flushInput)
rejected.reason: There is no per-byte loop to vectorize. The turn loop is syscall-bound (`Darwin.read` into one preallocated `turnStorage`, TerminalPTYHost.swift:456), feeds each slice straight through as an `UnsafeBufferPointer`, and the one bulk byte operation -- `Array(UnsafeBufferPointer(start: base, count: filled))` at line 2170, for the flight tape -- is already a `_platform_memmove`. `research/20` and `research/23` both characterize the drain as syscall and turn-boundary cost.

rejected.title: UTF8Decoder.next DFA table lookups
rejected.reason: Not vectorizable -- `state = Self.transitions[Int(state + characterClass)]` is a loop-carried dependency, one table lookup feeding the index of the next. Flagging it here because it is where the real non-SIMD win in this area sits: both tables are `private static let [UInt8]` (lines 8 and 27), so each of the two lookups per byte pays an `Array` bounds check that survives at -O plus a global-variable access, and the same Array subscripting is what would block auto-vectorization anywhere nearby. Moving them to a fixed-size `InlineArray` or a static `UnsafePointer` is a bounds-check removal, not a SIMD change, and it only pays on non-ASCII bytes since `T8` routes ASCII around the decoder entirely.

rejected.title: EscapeAbsorber.synchronizationPrefix builders (appendParameters / appendPrivateIntermediates / appendFinalIntermediates)
rejected.reason: These allocate arrays and format integers as strings, which would be indefensible in a hot loop -- but they run only when a stream-synchronization snapshot is taken, never during a feed. Not on any byte path.

rejected.title: SIMD UTF-8 validator as its own stage (simdutf-style block validate ahead of the decoder)
rejected.reason: It can coexist with the two contracts -- that is not what kills it. Resumability is satisfiable by never letting a block claim a trailing partial sequence (back off to the last complete scalar boundary, at most 3 bytes, and let the resumable UTF8Decoder own the tail via synchronizationPrefix); maximal-subpart replacement is satisfiable because a block validator's answer is binary, so any rejected block re-runs the scalar DFA from its start and produces byte-identical replacement positions. What kills it is that there is nothing to validate. The decoder is only reached for bytes >= 0x80: scrollback-stream, styled-screen-redraw and incremental-screen-updates are 0.00% non-ASCII (measured over benchmarks/fixtures/terminal-app.json), and unicode-wrapping's non-ASCII arrives in runs of exactly 12, 2, 15 and 4 bytes per line -- all shorter than one SIMD16 vector. Only synchronized-frames has runs long enough to vectorize, and there the useful work is not validation (the bytes are always valid) but scalar-boundary extraction and per-scalar classification, which is candidates 1 and 2. A standalone validator would be a third pass over bytes that are already walked three times.

rejected.title: terminalUnicodeClassification / graphemeBreakClass two-stage table lookup
rejected.reason: Gather-shaped, and ARM64 has no useful gather. `palette[Int(stageTwo[(Int(stageOne[Int(value >> 7)]) << 7) | Int(value & 0x7F)])]` is three dependent loads over 8,704 + 23,424 entries -- the stage-two index needs 15 bits, so it cannot ride a NEON vqtbl table lookup (16 bytes) under any packing. Batching N scalars gives N independent gathers, not one vector op. The construction audit reached the same conclusion from the other direction and explicitly declined to add a Latin-1 fast path in front of it ("a cache-shaped answer to a problem the run granularity already solved"). The one real win here is not SIMD: on a homogeneous run (btop braille is 147,463 scalars almost all inside U+2800-U+28FF, i.e. two stage-one blocks) the stage-one load is loop-invariant, so hoisting the block index across a run collapses three loads to two, or to one with a last-classification cache.

rejected.title: GraphemeBreakState.shouldBreak rule chain
rejected.reason: A branchy, order-dependent state machine over an 18-case enum with a carried look-behind -- it is sequential by definition and has no vector form. Its apparent profile weight is stale: doc 17's 1.99% on scrollback-stream (2026-07-29) and doc 10's 3.1-3.5% on styled-screen-redraw (2026-07-28) both predate the bulk ASCII run change (research/33/F16, 2026-08-07), which cut terminalUnicodeClassification on scrollback-stream by 180x and on styled-screen-redraw by 199.5x -- the bulk path calls neither the table nor the segmenter. Any current share is a small fraction of those numbers. The non-SIMD ideal (a 19x19 pair-verdict table so only ambiguous pairs consult the state) was already proposed as UNI-3 in docs/scratch/2026-08-18-construction-audit.md and deliberately rejected in its own Correction as "a larger structure, not a simpler one", with the surviving fix (rewrite the array-literal set membership as `==` chains) already landed at 4baa36f5 and visible in the file today.

rejected.title: canonicallyOrder insertion sort over the NFD buffer
rejected.reason: Search-only path (canonicalCaselessKey / canonicalDecomposition are reached from TerminalSearch key construction, never from Terminal.feed), and the input is one grapheme's decomposition -- the function's own guard `values.count > 1` documents that most calls see a single scalar. An insertion sort over 1-3 UInt32s with a table lookup per comparison is neither vectorizable nor worth vectorizing; the combining-class read is the same gather rejected above.

rejected.title: canonicalCaselessKey's three sequential passes over [UInt32]
rejected.reason: Three passes look like fusion bait, but each element's work is a two-stage table gather with a variable-length pool append -- data-dependent output length, so no lane-parallel form exists. Volume is also wrong: this runs once per search grapheme on a user-initiated search, not per fed byte. GeneratedCanonicalCaselessTables.record(for:) is already the same packed two-stage shape as the width table (stageOne >> 6 / stageTwo), so the binary search the audit complained about is gone.

rejected.title: TerminalScalars.canAppend's reduce over the cell payload
rejected.reason: `reduce(0) { $0 + Self.utf8ByteCount(of: $1) }` re-sums the whole payload on every append, which is O(n^2) over a cluster -- but n is bounded by Terminal.graphemeClusterByteLimit = 256 bytes and is realistically 1-4 scalars (research/12 measured 1,876 spilled cells in all of unicode-wrapping, 0.61% of cells). The hot print path does not even use it: appendToOpenClusterIfJoined tracks context.retainedUTF8ByteCount incrementally (Terminal.swift:8025) and the two `upToUTF8ByteCount:` callers are the state-synchronization decoder, a cold path. Vectorizing a 3-element sum is noise; the only defensible change is caching the running byte count, and the hot path already does.

rejected.title: TerminalScalars.utf8ByteCount switch
rejected.reason: A 4-arm range switch on a UInt32 that the compiler turns into two or three compares. It is called once per scalar on the probe path (TerminalInputStream.swift:121) where it only exists to cross-check the byte count the probe already advanced by -- so the right fix is to have the decoder report the consumed length directly and delete the call, not to vectorize a compare chain.

rejected.title: recoverClusterContextFromGridIfNeeded's scalar re-segmentation loop
rejected.reason: Loops over one cell's scalars re-running graphemeBreak to rebuild look-behind. Sequential by construction (each step feeds the next state), and the collection is a TerminalScalars whose storage is .single in the overwhelming majority of cells, so the loop body usually executes zero times. It is also called at most once per bulk run, not per character.

rejected.title: searchGraphemeKeys grapheme scan over the query string
rejected.reason: Runs once per search query over a handful of scalars typed by a human. Sequential state machine, and even a free speedup would be unobservable.

rejected.title: TerminalUnicodeClassification.isBulkPrintable's five-field conjunction
rejected.reason: Looks maskable (five booleans ANDed) but it is evaluated once per already-gathered classification record, so it is five register compares appended to a three-load gather -- the loads dominate and the compares are free. The real improvement is the one the construction audit already named at line 8630: have the generator emit isBulkPrintable as a field on the 30-entry palette so the predicate is a load rather than a derivation. That is zero extra table bytes and no SIMD.

rejected.title: appendBlankCells' constant-word fill
rejected.reason: Line 2878, `for index in 0..<count { chunk[base + index] = blank }`, is a textbook memset (the blank word is literally 0) -- but it is nearly unreachable. `appendRowPrefix` computes `stored = min(cellCount, row.cells.count)` and only calls it for `cellCount > stored`, while live rows are always materialized to full width (`GridRow(cells: (0..<columns).map ...)` at Terminal.swift:1822, 6396, 7226). The only producer of a short row is `truncateTail`'s width-1 hand-back. This refutes the first half of the prior pass's candidate 2: the loop exists, is SIMD-shaped, and does not run. The one-line `withUnsafeMutableBufferPointer { $0.update(repeating:) }` is still worth taking for free if the file is open for candidate 1 anyway, but it decides nothing.

rejected.title: recordsHoldTheSameContent's cell-word comparison
rejected.reason: Line 1914, `for word in 0..<count where left[word] != right[word] { return false }`, is exactly `memcmp` over two raw pointers, and its own comment says "this loop is what a whole-terminal equality spends nearly all of its time in" with research/31/F13 measuring 9.3% of whole-process CPU under ambient mouse motion. That evidence is historical: the same comment records that owner publication moved to the damage accumulator, research/33/F41 deleted `lastPlannedTerminal`, and a grep of `app/` and `lib/TerminalPTY` finds no production comparison of two `Terminal` values. It is a test-only value-semantics oracle now. Swapping the loop for `memcmp` is a two-line simplification with no production effect -- do it as cleanup, never as perf work.

rejected.title: forEachStyleId / forEachStoredCell full-arena word scans
rejected.reason: Lines 1999 and 2022 walk every retained cell word in the arena -- up to ~2M cells at the 15.75 MiB budget -- and the style scan is very SIMD-shaped (dedupe consecutive equal high-32 halves with one vector compare against a broadcast). Two reasons not to. First, research/33/F33 states plainly that "`F7` established that no calibrated workload contains the sweep trigger, so no paired benchmark was run": `reclaimDeadStyleEntries` fires only when the style table doubles past its threshold, which no benchmark reaches. Second, the per-cell cost is dominated by `Set<StyleId>.insert` in the caller (`liveStyleIds`, Terminal.swift:1753), not by the word load, so vectorizing the load moves a minority term. A scalar run-skip would capture most of what SIMD could, if this were ever worth doing.

rejected.title: forEachContentIdentity / forEachHyperlinkId table walks
rejected.reason: Same sweep trigger as above (research/33/F33), so the same no-workload-reaches-it verdict applies. Additionally the loops walk 4- and 8-byte side-table entries through `u16`/`u32`, each of which re-derives the chunk index and shifts a word -- branchy, variable-stride, and interleaved with a retained-window filter per entry. Fixing the addressing (borrow the chunk once per record) would dominate anything SIMD contributes, and neither is worth doing without a trigger.

rejected.title: withPaintedCells, forEachKind, forEachClosedRecordCell
rejected.reason: These are the three read walks the renderer, the geometry projection and the search index build use (lines 2109, 2198, 1761). They already do the thing SIMD needs done first: resolve the backing chunk once per record and read every cell through `withUnsafeBufferPointer`, with a comment (research/31/F13) recording that the bounds check and `immutableCount` load they removed were each named by a browse-frame profile. What is left is a per-column callback contract -- the caller keeps two or three decoded fields per cell and does its own work between calls -- so there is no batch to vectorize without redesigning the contract, and research/31/D3 Decision 5 chose the callback shape specifically to avoid materializing a `GridCell` per cell. Do not touch these.

rejected.title: hyperlinkId / contentIdentity per-cell binary searches
rejected.reason: Lines 2729 and 2758 binary-search a record's side tables once per decoded cell, which looks like a gather worth vectorizing. It is not: `record.hyperlinkCount` is 0 for essentially every record, which makes the loop zero iterations via `high = -1`; and a normally printed line has exactly one identity run, so the identity search is one compare. The `identityPerCell` encoding is already a direct indexed `u32` read. The branchiness is the point -- there is no vector to fill.

rejected.title: LogicalLineFold.enumerateRows' wide-cell boundary walk
rejected.reason: Line 394's walk probes `isWideHead` per cell and drives `recomputeIndex`, `lastRowRange` and `cursorAndRowCount`. A wide-head bitmask built with SIMD over the record's words would collapse the probe, and the probe is genuinely expensive (it reaches `word(at:)` at LogicalLineStore.swift:3486, which does a nested `chunks[i][j]` double subscript with no borrow). But `hasWideCells` skips the whole walk for any record without a wide head, so it never runs on ASCII workloads, and research/31/F9 measured the worst case -- the deepest wide history refolded at the 2-column minimum -- at 5.6 ms, inside one 60 Hz frame, which is why research/31/D3 Decision 7 shipped neither of its two mitigations. Reopen only if a resize-cost instrument (owed by research/32) shows otherwise; if it does, borrow the chunk before reaching for SIMD.

rejected.title: contentCellCount's wide-record kind count
rejected.reason: Line 1526 counts non-(wideTail|spacerHead) cells over a range and is SIMD-shaped, but it is guarded by `if record.hasWideCells == false { return range.count }` -- the header proves the answer for every narrow record, which is nearly all of them. Its caller is the search-distance path, and research/21 closed with double-click at 5.5 us and flat in history depth. Same latent addressing problem as above (unborrowed `word(at:)` per cell); same verdict that fixing the addressing, not vectorizing, is the first move if it ever matters.

rejected.title: RingBuffer.grow and RingBuffer.removeAll
rejected.reason: Lines 3606 and 3612 are element-copy loops over `ContiguousArray`, and `grow`'s masked read makes it a two-part `memmove`. Both are indexed by record count and block count, not cell count, and `grow` is amortized doubling. At the production budget the offsets ring holds tens of thousands of Ints, copied a couple of dozen times over a pane's whole life. Not measurable.

rejected.title: materializeChunk's zero fill
rejected.reason: Line 3183, `chunks.append(ContiguousArray(repeating: 0, count: size / 8))`, allocates and zeroes a whole backing chunk (64 KiB floor). The stdlib already lowers this to a calloc/memset; there is nothing a hand-written vector loop adds, and it runs once per chunk for the life of the store.

rejected.title: TerminalGeometry.swift and RetainedHistory.swift
rejected.reason: Neither file contains a loop over cell data. TerminalGeometry.swift is entirely public inspection value types with memberwise inits -- no iteration at all. RetainedHistory.swift is a 71-line mutation-door wrapper whose two methods call a body closure and re-synchronize a search index. Nothing in either file is a SIMD target, and I am recording that explicitly so the next pass does not re-read them.

rejected.title: Terminal.retainedContentEnd -- last-non-blank column scan
rejected.reason: Terminal.swift:6376-6385 is `row.cells.lastIndex(where: { cell in cell.kind == .narrow || cell.kind == .wideHead })`. Textbook SIMD shape, wrong substrate: `GridCell` is `CellWord` (UInt64) + ContentIdentity (UInt32) + HyperlinkId (UInt16), i.e. a 16-byte stride, so a vector load gathers half garbage. Worse, every caller on a read path is handed a row that `LogicalLineStore.paintedRow` (LogicalLineStore.swift:1659-1680) just built with two array allocations plus a `place` per cell -- the materialization is an order of magnitude above the scan. And it is not on the feed path at all: of its seven call sites, two are test-only (:3153, :3208), two are reflow-only (:6056, :6141), one is the OSC 133 prompt-redraw walk (:2247), and only `projectedCellEnd` (:4421) is a read path. The ideal fix here is structural, not SIMD: compute the content end from the record's arena words during the fold and never materialize the row -- at which point it becomes a reverse SIMD scan for the last word with kind in {narrow, wideHead} over contiguous UInt64, and worth revisiting.

rejected.title: Terminal.rowContainsContent and Search.lastProjectedContentRow
rejected.reason: Terminal.swift:8773-8777 is `row.cells.contains { cell.kind == .narrow || cell.kind == .wideHead }`, driven by TerminalSearch.swift:844-858, which walks the mutable suffix backwards once per `currentMatches` (so once per frame with an active search) and by Terminal.swift:4357 `stream.lastIndex(where: Self.rowContainsContent)`. Same 16-byte stride problem, and the row count is the viewport plus the open tail -- ~66-100 rows. Per the brief's own bar, a loop that runs once per frame over 66 rows is not a win, and each of those rows costs a `paintedRow` materialization that dwarfs its own scan.

rejected.title: Search.forEachSearchUnit -- the per-frame mutable-suffix cell walk
rejected.reason: TerminalSearch.swift:818-841 walks `row.cell(at: column)` and `row.scalars(of: cell)` for every column of every suffix row on every frame with an active search. It looks like the same loop as candidate 1 but it is on the opposite side of the projection boundary: `ProjectionRows.forEachRow` (Terminal.swift:588-619) hands it a `GridRow` that `paintedRow` allocated, and `row.scalars(of:)` returns a non-POD `TerminalScalars` per cell. There is no contiguous UInt64 to vectorize -- the words were already decoded into 16-byte GridCells one row earlier. The suffix is bounded by design (research/31/AR4), so the row count is small; the fix here, if one is ever wanted, is to route the suffix scan through the arena the way the closed half already is, not to vectorize the materialized rows.

rejected.title: detectedLink's http/https prefix window scan
rejected.reason: Terminal.swift:3874 `for start in lowerWindow..<upperWindow where hasHTTPSPrefix(scalars, at: start)` is a literal-prefix search over a contiguous `[Unicode.Scalar]` (POD UInt32) and is the most memchr-shaped loop in my area -- a broadcast compare for 'h' would skip most positions. It still loses: the window is built two lines earlier by `projectionUnits(from: Array(stream[firstRow...lastRow]))` (:3848-3851), and `forEachRowTextUnit` (Terminal.swift:4386-4398) heap-allocates an array per cell (`Array(row.scalars(of: cell))`, and `[" "]` for every padding cell) before appending a ProjectionUnit. The scan is a rounding error against the allocation that produced its input. research/21 reached the same conclusion about this call site from the other direction ('the bounded walk is small').

rejected.title: isActivatableWebURI's scalar predicates
rejected.reason: ActivatableWebURI.swift:27 (`scalars.allSatisfy(isDisplaySafeURIScalar)`), :110-132 (`isValidURIComponent`), and the `allSatisfy` chains in the IPv6/IPv4 helpers all look like byte-classification tables. Input is one URI, capped at 65,536 bytes but in practice tens to low hundreds of scalars, and it runs only on hover, arm, and open -- not per cell, not per frame, not per row. The non-ASCII half already escapes into `scalar.properties.generalCategory` (:98), a property-table lookup no vector op replaces. It is allocation-heavy (`Array(uri.unicodeScalars)`, `Array(authority)`, `Array(hostPort)`, `scalars.map(\.value)`), but that is a different fix and is not worth making either, at this call rate.

rejected.title: LogicalLineStore.forEachStyleId -- whole-arena style-liveness sweep
rejected.reason: LogicalLineStore.swift:1990-2005 is a whole-history scan over the same contiguous `chunk.withUnsafeBufferPointer` UInt64 words as candidate 1, so the substrate is ideal. But both production consumers are `history.store.forEachStyleId { live.insert($0) }` (Terminal.swift:1753, :3011) -- a Set<UInt32> insert per cell, whose hashing SIMD cannot touch. Style ids are strongly run-coherent, so the available win is a scalar `if styleId != previous` guard that skips ~99% of the inserts; a vector load buys nothing on top of that. Also adjacent to the style-run finder's area rather than mine -- flagging it so it is not lost, not claiming it.

rejected.title: NeedleWindow's binary searches in synchronizeIndex and refinedSearchMatchIndex
rejected.reason: TerminalSearch.swift:373-397, :431-441, and :564-574 are three hand-rolled binary searches over match arrays, and :1147/:1171 in the tests pin their instrumented visit counts. They are O(log n) over match counts, not cell counts, and the whole point of research/31/I7 (cited at TerminalSearch.swift:362-365) is that ordering the history-sized half folds nothing. Branchy log-n probes are the wrong shape for SIMD and there is no volume here to amortize it against.

rejected.title: TerminalDamage row-bitset word operations (formUnion, covers, fits, fill, translate, haloed, forEachRow, count)
rejected.reason: Confirms the prior pass's non-candidate call, with the reason made concrete: `TerminalDamageRowBits.words` is sized `(rowCount + 63) / 64` where `rowCount` is the *viewport height*, not a cell or column count (TerminalDamage.swift:341-344). A 66-row viewport is 2 words. Every one of these loops -- `formUnion` (:427), `covers` (:389), `fits` (:409), `fill` (:444), `translate` (:463), `haloed` (:547), `sameRows` (:568), `forEachRow` (:499), `count` (:351) -- iterates 2 elements. A 4-lane vector cannot help a 2-element array; the setup would cost more than the loop. `translate`'s doc comment (:454-459) already records that the word-level barrel shift replaced a per-row spelling worth +19% on scrollback-stream, so the structural win here is already taken. Note `Terminal.recordDamage` is genuinely hot (15.79% of scrollback-stream, research/17 F-table:331), but the work it does is `bits.insert(row)` -- one masked OR into one word.

rejected.title: renderRowReaches / renderApplyShape / renderTranslationStaleStrips
rejected.reason: Every loop here is bounded by row count, not cell count: `renderRowReaches` walks `plan.rows` (:78, 66 iterations), `renderApplyShape` walks `0..<rowCount` twice (:198, :239) plus a sort-and-merge over a handful of intervals (:223). This is exactly the case the task brief warns about -- a loop that runs once per frame over 66 rows. The element type is `RenderRowReach?`, a two-Int optional, so lanes would carry more branch than arithmetic anyway.

rejected.title: mappedGlyphs / positions per-cell accumulation in drawTextRuns
rejected.reason: Looks like the strongest SIMD target in the draw (positions for an ASCII run are an arithmetic sequence: fixed y, x = origin + column*cellWidth), and it is written once per *cell* at :1080-1086 and :1164-1169. It is already settled evidence, twice over. research/18/F15 (doc 18:988-1085) converted exactly these two buffers to unsafe pre-sized scratch, measured `faster` on two workloads (-2.98% scrollback-stream, -2.49% style-churn) and reverted it: 73 lines of raw-pointer accumulation in the renderer's hottest function for ~2.5%, judged an order of magnitude worse per unit of risk than the other landed leads. Second, the API forecloses the vector form: `CGContextShowGlyphsAtPositions` is unavailable in Swift and `showGlyphs(_:at:)` takes exact-count `[CGGlyph]`/`[CGPoint]` with no count parameter, so an over-sized SIMD scratch buffer would draw its stale tail. Third, the per-cell `guard glyph != 0` fallback branch (:1153) breaks the linear position sequence a vector fill would assume.

rejected.title: Per-cell sprite-family classification switch in drawTextRuns
rejected.reason: `for cell in run.cells` at :951 is per cell per frame and the routing at :968-1069 is a range dispatch on `scalar.value` -- superficially a SIMD classification. But `run.cells` is `[RenderTextCell]` (TerminalRenderPlanning.swift:379-390) whose `scalars: TerminalScalars` is an enum with a `.spill([Unicode.Scalar])` case (TerminalScalars.swift:39-43), so elements are non-POD and cannot be loaded as vector lanes without changing the plan's text representation wholesale. The routing is also already the optimized shape: research/17/F-era work replaced an ordered chain of eight range tests with a single floor comparison plus one switch, and the eight families occupy disjoint ranges. Also confirms the prior pass's 'sprite geometry' non-candidate.

rejected.title: Background / overlay / decoration run draw loops
rejected.reason: The three layer loops (:622-631 background, :634-643 overlay, :1462-1516 decoration) iterate *runs*, not cells, and each iteration is a `setFillColor` + `fill` into a CGContext that is a display-list recorder (research/18/F5). There is no arithmetic to vectorize -- the time is in CoreGraphics, and research/17's F-table puts `CA::CG::FillRects` at 0.37% of content-churn. The planner's run coalescing has already removed the per-cell granularity these loops would otherwise have.

rejected.title: overlayState linear scan over search matches
rejected.reason: `matches.first(where: { $0.columns.contains(column) })` at :98 runs per cell, so a row with many visible search matches is O(cells x matches) -- a genuine granularity mismatch worth noting to whoever owns search. But it is not SIMD-shaped: the data is `[(columns: Range<Int>, isActive: Bool)]`, a heterogeneous tuple array, and the fix is structural (the matches are already sorted and disjoint, so a single advancing cursor across the row, or a precomputed per-column overlay state, makes the scan O(cells + matches)). Reaching for lanes here would preserve the wrong algorithm.

rejected.title: LogicalLineStore.recordsHoldTheSameContent cell-word comparison
rejected.reason: `for word in 0..<count where left[word] != right[word] { return false }` at :1914 walks two raw `UnsafePointer<UInt64>` over the arena -- the most literally vectorizable loop I found, and the file's own comment (:1898-1904) says it is 'what a whole-terminal equality spends nearly all of its time in'. It is nonetheless not worth it: the same doc block (:1855-1857) records that whole-store equality left the frame path when owner publication switched to the damage accumulator, and equality now exists as a value-semantics oracle for tests. Additionally the ideal fix is a single `memcmp` over the run, not a hand-written SIMD scan -- libc's is already vectorized and handles the tail. If anyone ever puts this back on a hot path, that is the one-line change.

rejected.title: TerminalFrameBackingStore.translateRows pixel move
rejected.reason: The scroll translation of the IOSurface's pixels is already a single `memmove` of `survivorRows * rowBytes` (:231-235). Nothing to add; libc is the vectorized implementation.

rejected.title: Row-vs-row equality for dirty detection in the render path
rejected.reason: Listed in my scope and in the prior pass's hint #3, but it does not exist. Nothing in the render-plan or render-execution path diffs two frames' rows to derive damage: the terminal records damage at the mutation site (`TerminalDamage.record(row:)`), the planner consumes it via `reuseSource(_:)` (:291-297) to decide reuse, and `PaneFramePlanner` (:42) refuses reuse wholesale on a presentation or grid mismatch. `RetainedFrameRows` is copied by reference per row (:309-323), never compared. There is no loop here to vectorize because the design already avoids the comparison.

rejected.title: Color resolution (resolveCellStyle, resolveOverlayFill, overlayForeground, resolveCursorStyle)
rejected.reason: Confirms the prior pass's non-candidate call. research/33/F32 already moved this from cell granularity to run granularity: a 179x66 frame went from 11,814 `resolveCellStyle` calls to 66, one per style segment (docs/research/33.../findings.md:2942-2944), and research/17's F-table had it at 0.16-0.88% even before that. The per-run body is a short branchy ladder over three UInt8 components with brightness-separation search loops, which is neither hot nor lane-friendly.

rejected.title: RenderPlanRowSelection iteration and TerminalPresentation
rejected.reason: `RenderPlanRowSelection.Iterator.next()` (:576-583) is a bit test per row over at most 66 rows, executed three times per draw (background, overlay, text/decoration layers) -- ~200 bit tests per frame total. TerminalPresentation.swift holds no loop at all; it is four stored fields (36 lines). Neither is a candidate under any reading.

rejected.title: Background-run and overlay-run fills (CGContextFillRect / _platform_memset_pattern16)
rejected.reason: This is the single largest pixel cost in the process -- research/33/F26 puts `memset_pattern16` under `CGContextFillRect` at 3.62 s of a 10.60 s content-churn trace, ~34% of process CPU -- and it is already the optimal SIMD store. Our side of the loop is `setFillColor` + `fill(rect)`, one CoreGraphics call per run; there is no scalar byte loop to widen. The only lever is fewer pixels, and research/33/F36 already refuted that: submitting exact fill rectangles instead of the full frame moved fill samples per draw 1.521 -> 1.474, inside the trace's ~29-sample uncertainty, because CoreGraphics applies the clip before it writes bytes. T18 was implemented, measured, and reverted on both the performance lead and the structural bar.

rejected.title: translateRows scroll memmove
rejected.reason: `memmove(data + destinationRow * rowBytes, data + sourceRow * rowBytes, survivorRows * rowBytes)` is one libc call over contiguous IOSurface memory. `_platform_memmove` is already the tuned NEON path; hand-rolled SIMD cannot beat it and would lose the overlap handling. This is the research/33 T9 win itself and it is already in its final form.

rejected.title: Initial surface clear
rejected.reason: `memset(data, 0, byteCount)` runs once per backing store construction -- i.e. per swapchain rebuild on a geometry, font, scale, or color-space change -- not per frame. Already libc-optimal, and off the frame path entirely.

rejected.title: renderRowReaches row sweep
rejected.reason: `for (rowIndex, row) in plan.rows.enumerated()` with three `OptionSet.contains` tests per row. Exactly the shape the brief warns about: one pass over ~66 rows per render, three bit tests each, writing an `[RenderRowReach?]`. Nanoseconds against a bracket measured in milliseconds. The optional-element array is a bigger cost than the arithmetic, and that is an allocation question, not a SIMD one.

rejected.title: renderApplyShape interval build, span coalesce, and plan-row selection
rejected.reason: Bounded by damaged rows (typically 2-6 on `incremental-mixed`, 43-64 on live btop per research/33/F36), followed by a sort and merge over a list of that same length. The loop at :235 visits at most `spanRows + 2` rows per span. Nothing here is a per-pixel or per-cell quantity.

rejected.title: Swapchain per-buffer damage union
rejected.reason: `for index in buffers.indices { buffers[index].staleDamage.formUnion(damage) }` -- swapchain depth is small (>= 2), and `TerminalDamageRowBits.words` is `(rowCount + 63) / 64`, which is 2 words at 66 rows (TerminalDamage.swift:343). Two OR operations per buffer per publish. Confirms the prior pass's non-candidate call on TerminalDamage bitwords.

rejected.title: Sprite geometry rect generation (all eight families)
rejected.reason: Each family returns 1-4 `SpritePixelRect` values per sprite cell from integer division and branch selection -- there is no array to sweep. research/33/F37 vetted the adjacent idea (memoize box geometry, whose inputs are finite and repeated) and parked T15 because "the measured ceiling is too small to schedule"; a SIMD rewrite of the same arithmetic is strictly below that ceiling. Confirms the prior pass's non-candidate call.

rejected.title: TerminalFace ASCII glyph table and bounding-rect measurement
rejected.reason: The 95-entry `CTFontGetGlyphsForCharacters` / `CTFontGetBoundingRectsForGlyphs` pair and the `zip(resolved, boundingRects)` min/max reduction run once per face, i.e. four times per `TerminalRenderMetrics` construction -- on font, size, or backing-scale change, never per frame. research/18/F1 classifies these as once-per-metrics calls.

rejected.title: measuredInkEnvelope face reduction
rejected.reason: Four elements (`regular`, `bold`, `italic`, `boldItalic`), once per metrics. A SIMD4 max would be measuring nothing.

rejected.title: fillPatternedUnderline dash loop
rejected.reason: One `fill(CGRect)` call per dash across the run, so the cost is CoreGraphics fill-entry work, not the three arithmetic ops that compute each dash. Batching into a single `fill([CGRect])` would be the real change and it is lead L6's mechanism, not a SIMD one. Dotted/dashed underlines also appear in no benchmark workload.

rejected.title: emptyValuesKeepingCapacity dictionary walk
rejected.reason: Walks the retained keys of `shadedSpriteRects` (at most 4) and `legacySpriteRects` (a handful of alpha levels) once per text run to empty each bucket in place. The whole point of the helper is that it does *not* touch element storage. Nothing to vectorize.

rejected.title: RenderColor component conversion and setFillColor/setStrokeColor
rejected.reason: Four `CGFloat(x) / 255` divides per color, once per run, already passed as a stack tuple through `withMemoryRebound` with no allocation. research/18/F12 puts the surrounding cost in CoreGraphics' own dedup block (`CGColorCompare` at 5.4% / 4.0% as a leaf), which is lead L5's territory -- interning and hoisting, not lane width. A `SIMD4<Double>` divide would save three instructions per run.

rejected.title: TerminalFrameBackingStore.blit
rejected.reason: Has no production caller. The only call sites are FrameBackingStoreTests.swift:47,533 and FrameSwapchainTests.swift:45. Since T25 the surface is attached as `layer.contents` (SwiftTerminalSessionView.swift:497) and the render server textures from it directly, so no full-frame copy exists on the live path at all. Optimizing it would optimize the test suite.

rejected.title: ThemeRenderBridge palette conversion
rejected.reason: `theme.ansiPalette.map(Self.renderColor)` is 16 elements, converted on a theme change. Off any frame path.

rejected.title: AppKit chrome drawing (pane strip, dividers, drag overlay, chips, theme swatches)
rejected.reason: Reviewed all of `app/PaneStripView.swift`, `PaneDividerView.swift`, `PaneDragOverlayView.swift`, `ThemeSwatchViews.swift`, `PaneWrapperView.swift`, and `lib/ChipArtwork`. Every loop iterates a handful of chips, opcodes, or marks and issues CoreGraphics calls; none touches a pixel buffer, and none is on the terminal frame path. `ChipRenderer` draws at most a few dozen opcodes per chip image, cached per appearance.

rejected.title: Damage-clip construction in the view
rejected.reason: The brief names this as an area, but it no longer exists. T25 (research/33/F25) deleted `draw(_:)` entirely: `wantsUpdateLayer` is true and `updateLayer()` does nothing but count. The span clip doc 29/30 studied now lives inside `TerminalFrameBackingStore.apply` as one `context.addRect` loop over `shape.erasePixelSpans` followed by `context.clip()` (TerminalFrameBackingStore.swift:186-197), bounded by the damaged-span count (1-2 spans under btop per research/29/H1, up to ~ceil(rows/4) at the halo endpoint). Nothing there is a byte or cell sweep.
